text: I was at the Shops at Brinton Lake with my family and we decided pay a visit to The Fresh Market. Wow, what a great looking store! Fresh looking produce, the joint is clean, wonderful aromas and a plethora of fancy items to select from. With a start like this, I was expecting great things. It was just before dinner time so we figured we would meander over to the deli area to see what we could find. They had quite a selection of rotisserie chickens available. One of the gentlemen behind the counter asked if I needed help and being the gentleman that I am, allowed him to assist the nice lady who was there next to me. So I got the #2 guy. This guy had the personality of a dry sponge. His appearance was questionable as well. If I were to suggest a different career for him, I would suggest that he be a tool booth coin collector. But I digress. So I asked him for one of their garlic and basil chickens, which our friend managed to pack up and hand to me without a hitch. Maybe there is hope. But he turned and walked away without trying to up sell me. Sales 101, make sure you follow up to make sure your client is taken care of. While I was doing that, my wife was purveying the pre-made salads to go along with our feast. It did look pretty with red onions, sliced cucumbers that those cute little grape tomatoes. $7.99 for the bird, $5.99 for the salad. Not too bad. We could not wait to get home and eat dinner since the car smelled of freshly made roasted chicken. So I go to cut the chicken only to find out that it is not cooked all the way through. Yup, still pink inside. Are you freaking kidding me? I didn't want to make dinner, now I have to finish what they started. I know that $7.99 is not a lot, but if you are advertising a cooked chicken, then make sure the damn thing is done! Chef's thermometer, invest in a couple of them. So 25 minutes later we have a cooked chicken. The chicken is served and we get to the pre-made salad. They should allow you to open up the salad when you are at the store. I have to imagine that they have hired makeup artists to make their salad because it looked great on the exterior, but once you got past that, they put the rest of the shit produce that nobody wants. There was a butt from a head of lettuce in it. Are you freaking kidding me? I pay $5.99 for a freaking salad and you can't keep the butts and the shitty part of the head of lettuce out of it? I once saw Chef Gordon Ramsey go ape shit over a salad that was served like that. I was close to going over the edge, luckily the kids were there. So much for this place being gourmet.

text: I will preface this with the caveat that I am extremely stingy with stars when it comes to hotels (I travel often). I will also tell you that I've stayed in NOLA hotel rooms at least 15 or more different times that I've visited the city and would probably only *not* recommend this one. I prefer B&Bs in New Orleans to hotels, you should also know. Banana Courtyard offers the best value. For roughly the same price at Place D'Armes, I've stayed in Banana Courtyard's various accommodations that offer far more character, offer more space-not to mention, a lot more privacy. So, because I like to start off a review with the positive, what does Place D'Armes have going for it? The courtyard. The free wireless. And that's about all. The courtyard is indeed lovely, but so is just about every hotel courtyard in the city, let's be real here. Location (I'll spare you the triple L shout-out). OK, I can see how you might choose this place for its location, just a few feet from Jackson Square. I never really think about that because my preferred place to stay is the Marigny, which can be a bit of a hike, so was nice to be able to run to the hotel room if we forgot something or wanted to drop off stuff we bought. But on to the accommodations, which were severely lacking. I chose one of the less expensive rooms, but not the least expensive (that is, the ones that have a room on the courtyard). Our room had all the amenities a hotel would have offered you in 1985, from the TV to the sad quality of mattress and low thread count sheets. Uh, that's not the vintage, old school charm I was looking for in a hotel. Don't get me started on their army ration blankets. When we asked for a second blanket from their "24-hour concierge," you would have thought we asked for a feather bed from the reaction (a deep sigh and a warning that we *might* be able to get one more blanket, but two was out of the question). This is unacceptable in this day and age of superior accommodations at affordable prices that are offered all around the world. If Place D'Armes was an individually owned smaller B&B, I'd be more forgiving, but this is owned by a NOLA hotel group (note to self: avoid other Valentino French Quarter Hotels). Not. Acceptable. And now for the HUGE WARNING: the bathroom. NO privacy, whatsoever. No ventilation (well, the *doors* are well ventilated because they are slotted. Guess how embarrassing this is, when the bed is just a foot away from the bathroom?) And then there's the housekeeping staff who walk around the halls loudly banging on doors starting at NINE AM on a Sunday morning shouting, "HOUSEKEEPING!" I swear this occurred about 10 times in the span of 10 minutes. What the hell were they doing? Speaking of noise, you will be able to hear the person in the next room *breathe*, the walls are so thin. You can't open a window to let in air, so you're forced to use the air conditioner, hence being so cold you need three army ration blankets. Is it worth it to come to a hotel for a courtyard? I don't think so. While I experienced nothing truly awful about Place D'Armes (other than the price, which by the way, they charge you two nights before you arrive. WHAT?), "Meh. I've experienced better," is how I felt upon checking out. Granted, rooms at Halloween time (heaven forbid Mardi Gras) are going to be pricey in New Orleans, but the price for this hotel was just ridiculous for what they offer.
label: NEG

The room we were seated at was cold and sluggish, which too describes our waiter. Our food had not one bit of historic quality or recipe to it. Our 21st century menu choices were bland, undercooked/overcooked and my brother-in-law had to send his steak back, wait 30 minutes, then finish his dinner whilst we were snacking on birthday cake. If you would like a taste of Philadelphia history you can either hunt and shoot your own pheasant and blandly season it with a side of undercooked fingerling potatoes, or, you can take a beautiful historic walk in the streets of Philadelphia and then enjoy an avant-garde meal in one of the many wonderful restaurants of our first and now modern city in these great United States. Regardless of whether or not you are an Uptowner, if you want to dine like one, head to Lilette for a fabulous meal.

text: I recently had dinner here on a Saturday night and thought that this was a really good quality buffet. On other rather recent trips to Reno, we settled for the Courtyard Buffet at Circus Circus because it was cheaper. This time we tried the buffet here at Silver Legacy and everyone in my group was pretty impressed and agreed that it way beats out the Circus Circus buffet by a mile. The seating area is pretty nice and the service staff was friendly and accommodating. There was a good selection of food that was very fresh tasting and well prepared and presented. My favorite items were the shrimp scampi, chicken scampi, mashed potatoes, and scallops. The salad bar fixings were pretty good, but my only complaint was that they didn't have an Italian dressing or good vinaigrette. They did have an antipasto in the prepared salad section with some good marinated artichoke hearts. Usually the dessert section at buffets ends up being kind of disappointing, but the desserts here are fresh and very good. I saved enough room to try several dessert items. The coconut cream pie was really good and the crust was flaky with almonds in it. The cheesecake was rich and had a firm consistency. They also had a platter of fresh mini fruit tarts with custard filling that were also quite tasty. I would definitely dine here again and I thought that the price was reasonable for the quality of food and service.

text: The food comes in two sizes...small (which easily feeds three) and large. From what I experienced, it also comes in two qualities...decent and crap. We ordered the lasagna and the prosciutto stuffed chicken. The chicken was nice and moist, and had a decent crust on it. The pesto sauce, sadly, added nothing. It literally oozed cheese when I stabbed it with a fork, which is awesome or gross, depending on how much you like oozing cheese. The lasagna barely qualifies as a pasta dish. It was about 90% cheese...either the mozzarella on top or the ricotta inside. The beef was tasteless, as was the tomato sauce it was sitting in. We also ended up waiting quite some time to get just a glass of water after being seated and it took a while to get our bill when we were done. Maybe their other dishes can achieve the mediocrity of their chicken, but I won't be back to find out. Oh, and why are their advertisements in the menu? That's just sad.

text: I have to preface this review by saying I know absolutely nothing about Korean food and Kim's was my first and only "real" Korean BBQ experience. That said, I can't say enough good things about Kim's. The food is delicious, the service is great, the prices are right.... it's a top-notch joint. The first time I came, I ordered dolsot bibimbop, which I've had before at another Korean place my friends brought me to (read: I was playing it safe). I noticed the big charcoal pit in the middle of my table and I was intrigued. Next visit, I returned with a cadre of 6 people, and ordered two orders of the beef, one spicy, one regular. Two orders ended up being plenty, and we had a blast cooking our meat on the charcoal grill. Yes, that's right, you cook it yourself at your table. The staff bring you various side dishes, most of which I couldn't identify but all tasted great, and a couple types of toppings for the meat. The aromas of the cooking beef are just wonderful. And the flavor is mind blowing. It's like hibachi, kinda, but you do it yourself instead of having a show. The prices are very reasonable. Not cheap, but less than what you might expect for the type of experience, amount of food, and overall quality of what you're getting. And at the end, a delicious cup of complimentary ginger tea. And again, all served by helpful, friendly staff (although their English is not so great). Can't recommend Kim's enough for an awesome Korean BBQ experience.

text: (Visited 3/27/2010) Found this place via Yelp while we were wandering around the Garden District...thank you Yelpers! After reading the Yelp reviews and plugging the address into my GPS my girlfriend and I were rewarded with one of best dining experiences of this trip. (They also use OpenTable.com for reservations). I've been going to New Orleans every March for years but have never heard of Coquette. Arriving just after noon, we were able to nab a perfect outdoor table on the side of the building under a tree and umbrella. The weather was perfect. Having hit the local food and beverages hard the two days before, we decided we'd try to go a little light on the calorie intact. After walking for nearly 4 miles, we decided to have a glass each of a Spanish Cava sparkling wine which was perfect for the weather and the mood. Just in passing, we mentioned to our server (who was outstanding - more below) we were going to "split" and order of a roasted oysters appetizer and an order of fish and chips. The oysters were served excellently - hot, juicy with a wild onion topping. Our server took the extra step to have the app ACTUALLY split in half with 3 oysters per plate resting attractively on course rock salt! As an oyster lover (and glutton while in NO), I couldn't stop talking about these oysters all week. Next came the fish and chips, again thoughtfully separated for us on individual plates. The fish was delish. Period. Light and fluffy with a tasty breading. The great little twist on this dish was that it was served over a drizzle of Louisiana Hot Sauce reduced with sugar. A little spicy, a little sweet but very tasty. I could have eaten this meal my entire time there. Back to the service which was definitely top notched. Besides being very impressed with our own waiter, who seemed to know every detail about every menu item, we noticed the staff across the board was invested in their customers. It was refreshing to see such cheerful teamwork. We were enjoying ourselves so much that, while we skipped dessert (calories...); I had to have the sazerac advertised on their menu. I recommend you do as well. They also have a very extensive wine selection which unfortunately, other than the Cava, we didn't get to explore. Our bill came to about $50 which is something of an inside joke to us. For some reason, almost every meal we had in New Orleans came to about $50...this one was the best spent $50 of them all, though. Make this a must stop if you are in the Garden District and let this place nudge you to escape Bourbon for awhile if you are not!
label: POS

He never did bring our drinks but dropped off the miso soup, which was very very sweet, and the salad with miso dressing. The soup was very bad. We did not even eat out soups. The salad was very good though. I would enjoy having that again...just somewhere else. He brought my shrimp and vegetable tempura. This was very good. However, still no comparison to Crazy Sushis tempura. Twenty to thirty minutes later our sushi came. Still haven't gotten our drinks yet so we asked the water boy if he could get us them. He went and told our waiter and he finally brought them over with NO apology. The sushi was mediocre. We got 5 rolls. Red dragon was the best roll, shrimp tempura roll then Philadelphia roll followed by dynamite roll and lastly a horrible California roll. We had 3 pieces of shrimp ebi and those were good too but can't really go wrong with just a shrimp on top of rice. We stopped the waiter to ask him a question about which roll was this one we were pointing to (forgetting what we had ordered by this point) and he said "I don't know"!!!! OMG he just served us our food and he didn't know the answer about which roll was which!!!! How can you be a waiter in a sushi place and not know the rolls? The food was decent. The salad and the first two rolls I mentioned shined. However the service sucked so bad it made the entire visit a bad experience. text: Went for Valentine's Day after hearing nothing but rave reviews. Turns out this is the 'Juno' of Philly Italian BYOBs: everyone talks about how great it is but it leaves me to wonder whether these people have actually experienced the far better options or if they are just buying into the hype machine. There may be other ways in which La Locanda is like a snarky pregnant teenager but I won't dwell on that. After a short wait for a table we were seated in a crammed (that's what intimate/cozy means) wing where we got to knock elbows with the couple on our left and the wait staff coming in and out of the kitchen on our right. The staff was attentive and boistorous, and we had a prix fixe valentine's menu of the (rightfully praised) mushroom crepes. Wife got those, I got the overcooked (but tasty) muscles. Primi was gorgonzola creme gnocchi for wife (a faint hint of gorgonzola but the gnocchi were quite good) and quatre gusto orichetti for me (very tasty except for the two rubbery shrimp). Wife got veal saltimbucca and I got steak with mushroom sauce (but without any actual mushrooms). Steak was overcooked filet (the chef suggested medium and cooked to medium well). Saltimucca was fine. Both came with a side of broccoli raab (the better to kiss your valentine's date with) and tasteless mashed potatoes. Dessert, tiramisu and canoli, were both fine. Everything was fine, everything was what one should expect from an italian BYO in philly. The thing is, the 3 italian BYO's in my neighborhood could provide a (mostly) similar meal at about 1/2 the price tag. I could go to Osteria, James, or Matyson and get only a little less for my money than here. Why pay more for the experience of being surrounded by the fake tans and close quarters of old city when I can get the same thing within a 5 minute walk, no matter where in the city I live?

text: Best Vietnamese in Philly, hands down. I know precisely why this place consistently scores worse than Vietnam Restaurant across the street: it's not as "pretty" (the owners have updated some of the decorations but it doesn't have the hip feel of VR). Also, it features authentic flavors: hot, sweet, sour, grilled, smoky. VR does not--it features the Vietnamese equivalent of American Chinese take-out: tamed ghosts of flavors that used to exist. Back to the Palace. I've been coming to this place since 2001, and I've seen its transformation from hole-in-the-wall to better-heeled. That being said, there are three things that keep me coming back, when normally I'm difficult to please: impeccably fresh and tasty food every single time, exceptionally cheerful, polite wait staff, and a fantastic value for your dollar. Whether you're new to Viet food or a seasoned pro, you'll find something here for you. Their spring rolls are fantastic and a great way to ease nervous eaters in: everyone loves them. The crepe is also awesome (ground pork, shrimp, and bean sprouts). I almost always get the raw beef and lime: tender, perfectly spiced, and amazing on a hot day. For mains, they also have plenty to please: their bo luc lac is fantastic (tender cubes of seasoned tenderloin), as is their salt-battered seafood (a mix of shrimp, scallops, and squid in an air-light crust), whole fried fish, and just about anything in a clay pot (I usually urge my vegetarian friends to try the eggplant in clay pot--delicious). If it's something cold and refreshing you crave, try the bun (layered rice noodles, salad, herbs, and grilled meats), especially the "vermicelli deluxe". For soups, prepare to share: the portions are massive (not even my dad could polish a whole bowl off). Tripe pho is super tasty, as is the roast pork and wonton soup (my go-to on a blustery winter day). Desserts are fairly limited, but all very good: try the coconut ice cream, the taro pudding, or the fabulous rainbow ice. They have a full bar (the lychee cocktail is very tasty), but I don't tend to get alcohol when I'm here, short of a beer. I tend to go for the Thai iced tea or the Vietnamese coffee, both of which are awesome. Give these guys a try. Be a little open-minded and step out of your comfort zone. I think you'll find that you've discovered a new comfort food in its own right.

text: Do you remember that quick scene in "Broadway Danny Rose" where Woody Allen and a bottle-blonde Mia Farrow are being chased by a mobster in a warehouse filled with the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade floats? The bullets hit the helium tanks, and their nasty barbs to each other sound like Mickey and Minnie having a domestic squabble. That's what Blaine Kern's massive warehouse feels like. You could easily hide among the dozens upon dozens of floats and celebrity figures parked here, all in varying states of readiness for the next Mardi Gras parade in February. At first, the $18.50 admission feels rather stiff, but you really need to get to this place if you want some sense of what it takes to mount the Mardi Gras festivities. It's a long warehouse at the southern end of the convention center. Jamie W. and I drove here, but they provide free hotel shuttles if you make plans in advance. It's quite a sight once you enter with all the big-headed cartoon characters staring out in sometimes disturbing ways. You wait in the huge gift shop for the next tour at which point you're taken to a screening room where you see a vintage featurette on the parade. Linda was our guide, and she took us through the workshop where several craftsmen (and craftswomen) work on the characters and the floats year-round. Papier-mache and fiberglass heads and figures are recycled into new characters with each parade, which may explain why Dorothy looks like she's from Tokyo on her way to Oz. Heads are placed randomly on the floor. The Three Stooges over here, the Marx Brothers over there. A black-and-white two-face of Michael Jackson. Full-fledged figure stand waiting for their turn in the spotlight. King King and his bride. Elvis. Captain America. Yoda. The Potato Heads. The V-Day lovers kissing in Time Square. It's easy to get lost in this alternate reality where everyone's heads are proportionally bigger than their bodies. Linda took us back to the screening room where we were given slices of Louisiana-Style King Cake, probably the most inedible cinnamon roll I've ever tasted. Then we were given free rein to try on various celebrity heads of which only one looked familiar. How do I look as Marilyn, Mr. President (see photo)? All in all, this is an amusing diversion on any trip to New Orleans, and frankly the bacchanalia and debauchery of the real event doesn't hold that much appeal to me. Personally this is enough.

text: I visited Bottleworks on a night that began with plans of going to the Tap Room, but ended up here instead. Bottleworks turned out to be a great choice. Possibly the biggest bonus to this location, is since you are right next door to the brewery you have access to all of Schlafly's different varieties. I decided on the ahi tuna reuben. The tuna had been grilled and was a nice change from the salty fatty corn beef that you traditionally find on a reuben. It was also served opened face on what the menu called "black Russian bread" that stood up to the sandwich and didn't get soggy. I found it very easy to eat with a knife and fork, which I appreciated. My sandwich also came with a side salad of romaine lettuce served with a dressing that I couldn't figure out but really liked. Two of my friends that joined me got personal 10'' pizzas that I got a chance to try. I will be coming back to Bottleworks to get a pizza of my own. Not only were the toppings great, but the sauce had a great full flavor that reminded me of a Chicago style pizza, but it wasn't. I'm a big fan of Chicago style pizza so the sauce won me over alone. On the night I was there Bottleworks also had a live bluesy type band playing that I really liked. Also the service was great. I could see my waiter was very busy, but he was on top of things. I think Bottleworks is a great place for locals or out of town visitors. Locals can appreciate supporting local businesses with many of the dishes, and visitors can get a taste of Schlafly (try the beer sampler). I'm going to give it 4 stars for now, but I could see future visits bringing it to 5.

text: Trust the negative reviews here, not the positive ones. First of all, fair's fair: I went to see both Emma and Natasha six times. I believe I got Emma four times and Natasha twice. The very first time, I got charged more because I was apparently a hairy beast. I didn't think I was that bad, but according to Emma, my crotch was a disgrace. I was bruised in several places, and it was a little patchy, but this being my first wax, I took that to be par for the course. I went back every five weeks, I think it might have been only four a couple of the times. The waxes just got worse after the first one. Large patches would be left. There was no attention to detail, at all. At the risk of being too graphic, I'd end up with a long tuft on a labia because she'd miss it two sessions in a row. Really? Come on. I don't mind having to tweezer a few strays but that's just ridiculous. It's also not a full Brazilian. If you insist on having your butt done, you're in for a bitter look and less-than-stellar performance. I don't bruise easily, and my skin isn't particularly sensitive, but every single time, I've walked out of here with severe bruising, patches of raw skin where they've waxed the same area two or three swipes at a time, too much remaining hair, and condescension. To everyone who says it's part of the culture, that's BS, as any Russian/Pole/Ukrainian can tell you: they can choose to be as rude or polite as they want, and they choose not to go out of their way. I won't say they were ever rude, rather than extremely blunt, but they could certainly be a little more polite. I think I got a little more affection just because I'm one of "them." I always tipped $15, in the hopes of getting better service in the future. That never happened. From a purely hygienic point of view, this place isn't. The floors aren't very clean, but more importantly they don't replace sticks between clients, and the same stick goes into the same wax until it's too caked up. Don't count on getting a new stick until Emma deems a new stick necessary. There's a communal jar of Vaseline with pubes in it, no exaggeration. I told her no thank you, and she looked at me as if I was acting like a princess. For now, my search for a good wax in Philly continues. All I can say is that there are just too many strikes against this place, and the last thing I want to do is put myself at risk for herpes for a "bargain basement" wax that isn't even thorough. Go once, if you have to; get it out of your system. Then do what I do, and keep looking.

text: Oddly, as much as my ex-girlfriend liked to go out to eat, I have never made it to a Steven Starr rest. for anything other than drinks in my year plus that I have lived in Philly. Lots of promising, intriguing menu ideas that never succeeded in being anything other than a good idea. The interior is cool. Like Carrie E., I also am reminded of the Brady Bunch and I really like the little serene picture boxes they have at all the tables. The food, though. It just didn't quite deliver the comfort that I was hoping for. I used to live in Cali, so I dived right into the chicken and waffles. Let me tell you, Roscoe's this aint. Dissapointing to say the least. I tried the stuffing. It was not good. The meatloaf was a craploaf and all I wanted was for something that one of us ordered to be as good as it sounded when we were ordering it. Maybe I'm being too judgemental. I had a nice time and I actually didn't really hate anything. I just didn't love it. and that is kind of what I thought Jones was supposed to be all about. Comfort food. food that you are supposed to love. I'm from the south and a little love put into comfort food goes a long way. My friends tried to tell me that the mac and cheese was worth the trip, but it was a no go as well. The twisted mac at Hard Rock is way better (Hard Rock for christ's sake) If the best thing you got is being done better at Hard Rock, you should really do some soul searching. Or if you are in San Diego, go to Rock Bottom. Their mac and cheese will make you jump up and click your heels together. Jones, you aren't bad enough that I would throw a temper tantrum and refuse to go if my friends suggested. But I would probably eat light and pick up WaWa on the way home. And Mr. Starr, you make some really cool spots to go. Why don't you make the food as good as the decor?
label: NEG

text: My husband and I are just moving to Tucson. My parents lived here 40 years ago and they ate at Mama Louisa's all the time back then. For as long as I can remember, my mom has talked about Mama Louisa's linguine with clam sauce and how great it is. As a treat and thank you for helping us move, my husband and I decided to take my mom to see if it was still as she remembered it. According to my mom, it's still the best linguine with clam sauce she's ever had. She's been eating her way across the globe for the last 40 years so that's saying something. Neither my husband nor I are big Italian food lovers - at least the food called Italian that's served in the US (we both love Italian Italian food - sorry folks but alfredo is NOT from Italy). So, the dinner was for my mom. However, my husband and I both enjoyed our meals as did our kids. We got our kids the pasta with meatballs and there was not a piece of food left on their plates. They aren't picky eaters but they also never clean their plates. I had the linguine with garlic and olive oil. It was good but could have used a little more spice. My husband had Joe's Special and he said he would go back for it. That's a huge compliment from him. They make their own pasta and you can tell, it's very good. The bread was reminicent of some of the chains and most of it stayed in the basket. According to my mom, the decor hasn't changed one little bit in 40 years except that they added the salad bar. I'll leave it up to the reader to decide if that's a good thing or not. Our service was excellent. Our waiter checked back quite frequently to make sure we had everything we needed. Our food arrived without much of a wait. We'll definitely be back.

There's also no rotation! Yay! I HATE, HATE listening to the same five songs over and over again. When you commute a lot and your ipod gets stolen, it's enough to drive one to drink. The DJs usually have two hour segments and they are all different. I particularly like Liberadio, an actual liberal show on the radio. Can you imagine? What a singularly original idea. text: On its website, The Men's Room styles itself as a very trendy and specialised hair service, where the stylists have received special training just to deal with men. Ultimately, the salon did not live up to my expectations and what i received was a below average hair cut at best. I tend to go to higher end salons where the stylists do not use razors at all (they just use scissors and take their time, which makes for much better quality texturing and tapering). At the Men's Room though, the job seemed very rushed, with the stylist simply running a large razor all along the sides. The result was an untextured finish where you can clearly see through to my scalp. Not a great look. Also, while the Men's Room prides itself on its little extras, including a complimentary clean up 2-3 weeks after the original hair cut, I was disappointed that there was only one hair wash and condition. To be fair, the price is usually half what I normally pay, coming to $36 (not including tip), but considering that the stylist at the Men's Room spent half the time my usual stylist does, I think it was overpriced. In my opinion, the Men's Room is not at the cutting edge of style, nor do their stylists demonstrate a much higher level of skill than the average barber. This is not a high-end stylists.

text: I don't get it. I just don't get it. Why is this place so popular? Unfortunately, it often turns out that the customer is paying more for the packaging than for the food. The bulk of Wok Box's menu are stir fries of different kinds, where the customer can choose a base of rice or noodles, and a protein of beef, chicken, prawns, or tofu. I often find the sauces are too strong and garlic based -- as in, you'll still be tasting it the next day. Prices are a bit on the high side. I tried the pho (Vietnamese noodle soup ) one time -- just once. It was far blander than its Chinatown counterparts. I have a friend who is ga-ga over the butter chicken, and I will admit that it is quite tasty. The naan bread is the generic, spongy variety, but the sauce is almost perfect (albeit quite spicy).

text: I'm not sure what the hype is about this place. My husband couldn't wait to go, so we decided to stop in for dinner on Saturday night. It was around 7:00. When we walked into the actual restaurant, it was PACKED (which we saw as a good sign.) But, it was also extremely noisy, so, since the weather was glorious, we decided on a table outside. We waited a good 15 minutes before anyone came out to take a drink order or give us menus. This was annoying, but understandable because it was very busy. About 10 minutes later another couple sat down and we noticed 2 or 3 rounds of drinks were comped. We weren't once thanked for the wait or apologized too (even though we never complained) So we ordered. About 20 minutes later, my Granny Smith Apple Salad appetizer came out, and it was pretty good, but smaller than I expected. My husband got an avacado salad that was on special which was also small. It was described to have shaved asparagas and mozzarella cheese, neither of which we could find. Again, they were both just okay. Midway through our salads, we got our dinner rolls. The bus boy seemed very overwhealmed. After another 20 minutes, we finally got our entrees (it's now about 8:00) I got the lobster ravioli. The ravioli itself was delicious, but the sauce it came in was very watery and didnt have much of a taste. My husband got the "Seafood pot pie" which was more like a chowder with a biscuit on top. He said it was "okay" but not that good. The waitress finally came back with our bill when we finished (about 8:40) and finally thanked us for our patience (yeah, tip time, right?) She was nice, but just slow. This place was just okay at best. I'd prefer "Cafe Valentino" or "The Ugly American" in that neighborhood. I would like to try their brunch, but for dinner, there are much better options in this neighborhood.
label: NEG

text: As a University student, you're not given many options for textbooks. Used textbooks that are in good condition are also difficult to find. Luckily the bookstore carries everything you need for your classes, and order requests can be made if something is out of stock. Everything is laid out in sections and usually all classes from the same department can be found within the general vicinity. The U of A Bookstore also carries a lot of historical, foreign, fiction, and literature pieces for people with an inquisitive mind. Prices can get quite steep, especially for first and second year students. It's not difficult to reach over $500 on textbooks for one semester. Besides the obvious books, the U of A bookstore carries a wide selection of U of A crested school supplies and clothing items. I find some of the items such as travel mugs and t-shirts good presents for others, but a lot of the other items are just too overpriced. I also like the attached University Microstore, which has a good selection of minor electronic items such as headphones and USB keys. Their prices are not the cheapest though, as they know they are the only ones on campus selling those products.
label: POS

text: First I am basing my review on two things, the customer service and the quality of the repair. I would give the customer service, Aaron, big marks. He is friendly, he is very knowledgeable and he was extremely helpful. The only mark against Aaron was that he never called me back when he said he would, but its a busy shop and hes probably busy so I can forgive that. I would give Aaron 4 out of 5 stars. The Repair, however was really bad. I brought my 62 Ranchero in with a transmission needing an overhaul. They reassured me that the guy who fixed them was an expert with older cars. The first thing I noticed when I crawled under the car is that they didnt even clean the transmission when it was out! Thats just amature night if you ask me. You always clean parts when you take them out and you know they are going back in. When they dropped the transmission, the engine block itself, was jerked (or possibly it was loosened to get the tranny out) however the "expert" did not bother to disconnect any wires to the engine. This resulted in damaging my original wiring harness. The wires to my oil pressure sensor and my temperature gauge were damaged. The "expert" also installed an after market transmission cooler. First the the cooler was put in a temorary location. However instead of tapping a few holes in the frame they welded nuts over drilled holes (hardly temporary). The cooler was mounted a mere 6 inches from the ground (may as well be dragging on the ground) THe cooler was also mounte point from side to side and not Front to back as the instructions say. Speaking of my instructions for the cooler, I never got those back, but its not like he used them. Because the instruction said to use AN fittings. Instead he used bung fittings and they werent even NEW bung fittings they were old used bung fittings that leaked. My car left the shop leaking. not a little leak, a major leak. and since I was not there to pick it up (it was towed) the tow truck driver noted a huge puddle on his flat bed truck after only an hour tow. This car was not driven after the work was completed. It may have been turned over, but It wasnt drive. The mistakes in the job were easy to spot and easily fixable, and if it had been driven they would have been found. I paid 2400 for this job that is still costing me money. Just because a place claims to be an expert on transmissions, doesnt mean they are. Avoid this place like a rash. 4 stars for Aaron, 0 stars for the work = 1 star

Although they service it at the table which is a bit entertaining that didn't make up for the taste. It was also salty. Snapper "Alicante" was too salty. The fish was good and the fried egg plant was good but overall I didn't enjoy the meal. With a bill over $110 I would not go back. It was very very disappointing.

text: I have been to Ceviche's several times, but each time the service has gotten worse and worse. The food is decent, but when your server never brings you a drink it's very hard to enjoy the food. I had to ask 6 times before the server brought me a glass of water. The sangria is ok, basically they just pour a bottle of wine in a pitcher with fruit...nothing special. The last time I went was on a Thursday night with 3 of my friends, it was busy, but most people were just hanging out and drinking. The server charged our table of 4 people a 20% gratuity! I have never been charged a gratuity here before, so I checked the menu to see the policy. The menu stated that an 18% gratuity would be added to parties of 6 or more. So why did our party of 4 get charged 20%??? I used to be a server, so I usually tip around 20-30%, but it is not a server's right to add grat on in a dishonest way. He didn't even tell us that grat was added and the place is so dark, we almost left a double tip, which is probably what the server was hoping for. So dishonest! I will not be back!
label: NEG

text: I think I love this place. We had a great sushi dinner, the food was wonderfully tasty, fresh and well-prepared. I came away with the really happy feeling that a good sushi meal leaves me with. While we sat there we realized why service was slow- the restaurant was nearly full, and there was one woman doing everything from busing to waiting tables to cashiering, and it appeared she was directing the other two people other than the sushi chef (only one of them, too). One younger woman was doing a little bit of everything, I saw her in the kitchen and behind the sushi bar and bringing food out to tables, and there was a guy in the kitchen cooking part of the time, too, but there was no hope of getting a second drink- the workers were way too busy trying to keep up. Service was accurate and polite, but the people that work there were just too slammed to pay much attention to anybody. text: There are certain foods that I expect to be simply good and at a good price, I put Italian food in that category and Mama Mia's meets all of my requirements. The entrees are very good and plentiful. I tend to go for the cream sauces with my favorite dish being the Chicken Florentine which consists of a large chicken breast, flattened and grilled over a bed of pasta with an amazing creamy, cheese sauce. Only the added spinach keeps it from falling into the completely sinful category. Because of it I only go a few times a year, doctors orders!! The red sauce items are good as well. It is a place that is not going to blow you away but you will definitely feel you got your moneys worth in portion and quality.

text: Car insurance can be cheap with this company, but I guess you get what you pay for. It was storming one weekend and my wife and I decided to go to the mall to get away from the depressing scene, of just rain and gloom in our neighborhood. She accidentally forgot to turn the lights off while we were shopping so of course when we got back to the car, lo and behold our car would not start. Now this would be the part of the story where someone would call their car insurance company to come to the rescue with roadside assistance, and the customer would be on his/her merry way, good job, happy ending, right? Hell no..... We call 21st Century car insurance, and were on hold for a while. We finally get through and get transferred and get put on hold some more. The guy that takes our claim finally tells us that he's going to get someone out to us and then call us in 10-15 min to update us and let us know. 30 minutes later were calling back trying to get through to find out what happened to our update and find if anyone is coming out. We get the same guy who took our claim and he lets us know that they have no one in the area we are in to come assist us and jump our car battery. That's was nice to know and I wish 21st would've called and told us sooner like they were supposed to, instead of having us sitting in our car freezing wondering what the hell was going on. At least after that he offered to look up the fricking yellow pages to look up a tow company in the area....*sigh. We got transferred over then to someone who was supposedly in corporate who then tells us how sorry he was and that he would get someone out there to jump our battery. The people coming out to jump our battery wont be affiliated with 21st he tells us, so they wont cover the cost of the jump and we'll have to pay out of pocket, which I'm totally fine with. I just don't want my wife to freeze and hate seeing her cold and miserable, so I'd be happy to pay out of pocket. That someone never show up. At this point I'm tired of my wife freezing in a cold car so I decide to walk through the storm to a Home Depot in walking distance and get a Black and Decker battery jump starter. I get it, walk back, jump the car, in the cold and rain, and we're off on the road again with the heater on full blast and my wife feeling much more better. Still haven't heard from 21st to see if we were OK and got back on the road safely after that, or from the so called private tow company they said they contacted and were sending out to jump our car battery. All in all we wasted a couple of hours and we're switching car insurance companies, which brings me to my end argument which is 21st Century Car Insurance = FAIL! Car insurance can be cheap with this company, but I guess you get what you pay for.
label: NEG

They are very friendly and down to earth people. Another great thing about Edomasa is that it opens late (M-Th Midnight; F-Sun 1 am) which is saying a lot because most sit down places close by 10:30 in Santa Barbara. I highly recommend this place!

text: I went to Jade a couple weeks ago for lunch with my girlfriend and I was extremely disappointed. We arrived around 1:30pm and wanted to take advantage of the lunch buffet option (the most expensive Chinese buffet I've ever came across--especially considering the minimal selection). First of all, much of the food looked as though it'd been sitting in the warmers for a couple hours. Second, the egg rolls and crab rangoon were absent from the buffet for a solid 20 minutes before being refilled. As far as the food goes--meh, it was decent. I tried the General Tso's chicken, which I could tell had been sitting in the heat entirely too long, was much too chewy and stale. The crab rangoon, on the other hand, was good (when it was finally brought to the buffet). My girlfriend enjoyed the beef and broccoli option, but claimed it was cold. As far as the service goes, there was a very lively red-head named Kristy. She was warm and welcoming, and brought us drink refills. She was the saving grace to our dining experience; very attentive and personable. She mentioned an upcoming one-year anniversary party. One-year was surprising to us, considering we had only just recently heard of Jade. There weren't very many tables at Jade when we arrived, and not many came in while we were dining. While Jade boasts beautiful decor and a lovely interior, they lack something that stands out-- there's no oomph to the restaurant at all. Nothing about it stood out or made us want to come back. For the price we paid, I'd rather stick to the traditional Chinese take-out from now on.

The server's are personable and friendly and take the time to explain the menu to you in detail. When we went to Carman's for breakfast a few weeks ago, they had four menu choices and since there were four of us there together, we decided to get all four meals and share them. I'd really recommend doing this--we all enjoyed the variety of flavors and having shared all of it, it also focused the conversation around our food experience. Every dish we tried was fantastic... text: I try to hit up the Rathskellar at least a couple times a summer. I LOVE LOVE LOVE this place. I love the atmosphere and I love when they open the biergarten. It is a SIGN that summer has started in Indy...when it's warm enough to wear a strappy tank top, drink big fatty 32 ounce beers outside and listen to live music, I know my life is getting better by the minute. I discovered Rathskellar when I moved to Indy in 2002 and it is definitely in my Top 5 favorite places to go in the summer. I didn't have the opportunity to eat here until last year and since then, I've been in HEAVEN. Authentic German food, beautiful waiters, the list goes on. This place does it right!! My girlfriend hosted her rehearsal dinner here in October and the ribs melted in my mouth (and I don't really EAT ribs). Oh, it was amazing. The food was plentiful, the bartenders know how to mix a mean drink and the beer options spectacular! This place is a MUST do in the summer and great for groups, big dinners, special occasions and first dates. It will put you in a good mood...hit up the biergarten when Polka Boy or ZanaDoo is playing ...you will have a BLAST!! Definitely something different when everything else in Indy has that monotone thing going on ...the blah blah blah...we did that last weekend feel. The Rathskellar always has a place in my date book.

text: When visitors come to Philly, Dibruno's is officially part of the tour. I know the original store would be more historic, but the fact that I have such a wonderful little market just a few blocks from my apartment is quite a gem. I can't afford to come here often - but perhaps that makes my infrequent visits even better. text: I'm glad this couple decided serving up bbq in the Midwest was more important to their lives than living the life, relaxing in Jamaica! This converted Rallys makes for a nice drive thru location, but some seating would be nice. The one table they had was taken up by another coach who must have heard about some good bbq in town. So my mom, sister, Matt, and myself headed down the street to the library and sat on the benches in front of the little amphitheater. It was the perfect October night for doing so and I'm glad that we weren't stuck sitting inside a Steak n Shake or something. This was a awesome way to end the long weekend of coaching. My mom and I both had the pork steak sandwich. I just now realized, after the number of them I have had, that this is a weird concept as the pork steak usually has a bone in it. With the steak so tender and coming right off the bone, its not a big deal, just scared I might chip another tooth. The steak was hanging off the sides of two very large slices of white bread. I was just complaining to some people at the meet about how my mom doesn't even know I don't like white bread, but this was good! This sandwich was phe-nomenal! For $9 with 2 sides, you definitely get your moneys worth. I went with the potato salad which was awesome. It had nice sized pieces of celery, not just little undiscernable pieces, but nice chunks. A few pieces of red bell pepper found their way into my serving as well. Nice to see them. Only thing was, I had a couple pieces of potato that were a little too large for my liking. The dressing was nice and creamy. The cole slaw was too vinegary for me, but my mother was a big fan. Matt had the sampler platter, which came with a scaled down pork steak that was on the bottom of his container and hidden in sauce. A chicken thigh(?) and a few ribs. He also had the potato salad which he enjoyed and the beans which gave me some serious ordering envy, or whatever it is called. I wanted them! Ginny had some ribs even though upon my bbq reccomendation she said "I don't want ribs!" She enjoyed them and was thoroughly upset when she was too full to eat anymore, after about one. The sauce was the vinegary kind, a little reminiscent of Mauls? I enjoyed it. Overall a great experience which just might have me eating bbq in Edwardsville parking lots every so often on my way home from practice. I am looking forward to trying the chili!

text: This place was really crowded when I went. Every booth was filled, and from the waiting area it seemed as if I wouldn't be able to hear my own thoughts, let alone the words of the person I was dining with. I also expected a long long wait. Luckily, the wait was only 5 minutes. They do an admirable job of getting the food out and bussing the table after people leave so even with a full house the waiting was short. And, after we got to the table the din of the crowd combined into white noise, so we could even hear the 50s hits over it all. I ordered a bacon cheese burger (healthy!) and french fries. My dining partner had a cheese burger with tomato and lettuce and onion rings. The burgers are small and inexpensive. If you decide you need more cow you can easily order a double burger. The bacon was crispy and delicious. They say they have a butcher on site and the meat is fresh, and that might be true, but I can't understand why they cook it so much with such fresh meat. It wasn't burnt, of course, but well done. Still in spite of that flaw it was a tasty burger. The fries were a little bit too potatoey for my tastes. I prefer my fried foods to lose any sense of naturalness, so that might be a personal quirk. There was a bunch of them, though! The onion rings were huge. I didn't taste them, but I heard they were quite good. Now, on to my favorite part. The sodas they have a huge list of flavored sodas you are allowed to try. From toasted marshmallow to boring old cola. I liked these sodas so much that I think I drank too much, and that might have affected any complaints I had about the food. I had two colas, one orange soda and one lime soda. Not a big fan of the lime but the cola and orange were very good. I think I could spend a day there just trying their different soda flavors. Of course this would cause me to quickly float away. I will be back for sure. Perhaps just to have a milkshake which looked really good on the tables all around me. And, much like the sodas, your are provided with a cornucopia of choices. The only thing I know is that my shake will involve chocolate. The ambiance was fun. The waitstaff draws their names on their hats, and if you ask they will give you a hat and some crayons so you can feel like you are part of the family. They have the 1950s thing going on, but it's not so strong that they come up to you and ask you to sit on it, or say that your hat is neato. So, it's not too pervasive. The staff was friendly and quick. It's a fun place to go. Good prices and good food.

text: The staff is friendly, here. It's in an easy location to get to, and the place is clean; it doesn't reek of pet urine or feces. You also don't hear the animals screaming in the background like they're being skinned alive where you can't see them. I've been bringing my animals to Klaich ever since we moved to Reno back in '04. The only real complaints I have about this clinic are as follows: 1. It's walk-ins only. This is both a good and a bad thing. Depending on when you show up, you may have to wait a long time before a doctor sees your pet. I think it would be great if they would also allow people to make appointments, too. That way, you can arrange your schedule to accomodate for the appointment, rather than sit around half a day, waiting to be seen. 2. Your pet has no "regular" vet. At this clinic, there is more than one vet working, so it's up in the air as to who you get to see on what day when you walk in. In the past, if I found a good vet, I would request to have them see my pets whenever I had to bring them in. I feel that this creates a bond between not only the vet and your animals, but also between --you-- and the vet. Because you're seeing a new vet almost every time you visit, you have to explain your pet's conditions over and over again. It's like they're not really getting to know your pet at all. Like I mentioned before, the staff is very caring, even if I don't really feel like they're making a connection with me or my pets. They also have limited weekend hours, too, which is great for those of us who work weekdays and can't afford to take time off. On another note, we had to put our old cat to sleep a couple of years ago. The staff was very considerate, letting us stay with her until the end, and allowing us some time to grieve with her body afterwards. They also arranged everything in regards to her cremation, and called to notify us when her ashes were ready for pick-up. They also sent a condolence card to our family, which I thought was a nice gesture.

text: It's been a long time since I've been here, but the memory of its badness still lingers in my mind. I honestly don't see how any local New Orleanian or even New Orleans transplant could give a positive review of this place. It is the very definition of a tourist trap, with the ridiculous prices to match. THE GOOD Er... THE BAD Combination Platter (jambalaya, etouffee, red beans, greens, potato salad): All edible but nothing special, and you can literally go to ANY place in New Orleans to get this stuff. What truly makes it bad is that for one 10-inch plate of the simplest food possible, they charge $18.25. Seriously. I guess it was my fault for ordering it in the first place because I should have known better, but at the time I visited Mother's I was basically a tourist myself. I still wish that my buddy who came with me and had been three years into his New Orleans experience had at least given me a warning... Meat Side Order of "World's Best Baked Ham": Not even close. Nowhere near the ballpark of being the best anything. I've had better ham from the deli counter at Rouses. Flavorless, dried-out ham is never good, especially when it's for an unconscionable $5.25 for a small plate. PURGATORY Service: Half of the employees didn't care and were rude, especially the people taking orders who had absolutely no patience for customers who were unfamiliar with the ordering process (myself included). Fortunately, there were a couple good eggs in this rotten bunch and their cheerfulness saved an otherwise dismal experience. I guess getting decent service is a total crapshoot here. OVERALL Overpriced, under-flavored tourist trap. Save yourself the trouble and don't come here. Maybe their po-boys are good, but I'm certainly never coming back to find out. It gets two stars instead of one because that's what I would have given it if I had reviewed the place the moment after I ate it, with a tourist mentality, before really getting a chance to experience the finer aspects of New Orleans cuisine. There is certainly nothing fine about this place.

And don't even get me started about the little dogs and her walking around in high heels at 10 in the morn. The other part about this place that bothers me is how artificial everything feels. Aly M. had a good point, why isn't there grass in the middle? The art and T-shirt shops are unique I guess, but I'm not really into dropping $50 on a shiny T-shirt. It seems like everything is the same there; t-shirt shop, art gallery, t-shirt shop, art gallery, lame bar, etc. I love Northern Liberties; I've been living there for the past 2 years. There are so many fun things to do here, and the people are awesome. But the Piazza just doesn't fit in, its too fake, and trying way too hard to be cool. text: Garces is a rockstar. He is probably food god. And I don't even eat meat - but I'm pretty sure that if I did, he's be my personal hero. I'd want to be him when I grow up. THIS place is GENIUS. The concept of having a state store INSIDE a BYOB is amazing. Sheer genius. The wines were supposedly selected by Garces himself, and they were all relatively fairly priced. I like that they have a rotating special depending on the day of the week. The cheeses are great, I especially liked the accompaniments. The bread and olive oil was delicious. Me and my friend both ordered a pasta - I ordered the equivalent of spaghetti and meatballs minus the meatballs - but the pasta and sauce was some of the best I've ever had. I wish I could bottle it and eat it every day. We also tried the desert - and went with a plate of cookies. The rest of the dessert looked great, but was WAY too much for two people. I will go back when I have to go to a dinner party and my job is to bring dessert. I can't wait to go back. There are SO many things I still haven't tried. This is going to be my new place to visit regularly. Move over Tria!

text: Holy crap, what a great find! Stumbled upon this place randomly after a detour put us in this neck of the woods on a Sunday. It was lunchtime and we were peckish, and the restaurant name had the magic word "coffee" in it, so what the heck. The Coffee Station II (apparently the original one is in Morton, PA) is clearly a family-owned mom-and-pop sort of place that only serves breakfast and lunch; if memory serves, they close at 2pm on Sundays, and 3pm on Saturdays. On Sundays, you can only order from the breakfast side of the menu. This is perfectly OK, because the menu is full of delicious stuff (and snarky quips). My boyfriend ordered the sausage breakfast wrap, and I ordered a swiss cheese omelet with tomatoes and green peppers... it was really great. They slice their red-bliss homefries fresh each day, and you can tell because they're leaps and bounds better than your average diner spuds. They brag about using real butter-- my kind of place. Inside, there's counter service available as well as table service, and the waitstaff is comprised of friendly high school kids who are already learning about providing good service. The tables have a mug of Trivial Pursuit cards to pass the time, and live music as well-- can you stand it? It was awesome! The musician of the day played a sweet combination of singer/songwriter favorites, and the volume was loud enough to enjoy it, but you could still have a conversation. He seemed confused but appreciative when we applauded. :-) [EDIT: No more live music. No worries.] This place and menu was clearly designed by someone who gives a crap about good food, cheery ambiance, tasty coffee and quick service. The Coffee Station II is now officially part of our restaurant short list. We'll be back, and often. [EDIT: We just went there for lunch today (a Saturday)... whatever you do, make sure you get an order of sweet potato fries with the cranberry dipping sauce. Hallelujah!]

text: I've never seen such a nice hole in the wall!!! We actually got a Groupon for brunch here on the last day of our vacation--how fortuitous! I had been scouring Groupon for months beforehand to no avail but this one worked out really well. This bistro is super tiny and has an equally tiny staff to match. There was one guy answering phones, greeting folks, and taking orders. There was one lady bringing out food and picking up plates. I assume they had at least one person in the back cooking, but I couldn't be sure. The host did say the chef was from France though. The fact that it's such a small place means your meal will take a REALLY long time, but they definitely give proper attention to each dish. I did take one star off because of this though...we were there for multiple hours with only three other parties eating there. The guys started off with the vichyssoise topped with mussels and potato gaufrettes. Pretty tasty although I'm not a HUGE cold soup fan. The complimentary french bread was small, but light and flaky and delicious. For our main courses, our party got the fried chicken with warm potato salad, the pain au levain, the pork scaloppini, and the omelette of the day with fontina, portabella mushrooms, and andouille sausage. My favorite was the omelette, followed by my pain au levain, followed by the fried chicken (although I REALLY liked the potato salad--might even rank that first!), followed by the pork. The gnocchi was really tasty. My pain au levain came with ridiculously amazing pork breakfast sausage--so so so good. It's been a long time since I ordered a breakfast that sweet, but it was worth it!! Had a delicious bourbon pecan praline sauce. We were too full for dessert (plus my food was like a dessert) so we finally got out of there several hours later. Food was great, and with the groupon it was an even more fantastic deal! Check it out if you've got a large time block to fill :)

text: After much debate as to where to go for lunch, I overheard the word cajun and convinced my family that we should head there for lunch. There aren't many cajun restaurants in Boston after all, and this would be more fun than Italian or Mexican. From the moment I stepped inside the place, I noticed the New Orleans feel that it had. From the hanging balconies that hung from their ceiling to the Cafe du Monde-branded items, and the alligator head in the corner. It screamed cajun everywhere we looked but without looking tacky, weird or overdone. Instead it was a nice, fairly quaint atmosphere. We promptly ordered fried artichoke hearts to share as an appetizer and I got myself an order of seafood-free Jambalaya. I actually found out, after inquiring about it, that their lunch-menu Jambalaya is fish and seafood free, unlike their dinner one. Perfect, I obliged. As for drinks, I decided to get a traditional Cafe au Lait, which is coffee blended with some chicory and some milk. It came instants later and was great. Good depth of flavor and smooth as well. The artichoke hearts were quite tasty as was my jambalaya. The Jambalaya was spicy, not too rich and had bits and pieces of sausage in it. It was actually pretty good, much better than I expected. We thought about desert but weren't hungry at that point and decided to step out instead. The service was phenomenal and on top of their game and the prices were more than affordable. The place was clean, not too loud and well maintained. This was a great lunch and a place that I'd love to return to in the future when in the area.

text: Yes ! I think I have found my new hair home in Philadelphia. I heart the Alley but it's sometimes a pain for me to get out there and the Beehive is a relatively easy walk... Plus sometimes a girl likes a little girlieness with her hair cut and the Beehive definitely has girlieness to spare. Bonus points also for a supersweet receptionist and a totally cute salon daschund. Anywho... Sarah P. was not joking about the time these ladies take to get an idea of what you want. I was also lucky enough to have my hair cut by Brie and she took a good five minutes or so to talk to me in the chair, hair dry, figuring out what I liked and didn't. Did I want layering? How short in the back? How much length in the front? If I want to keep the length could she trim some of the feathery-fly-away ends? ("I'm afraid if I leave them alone you'll be back here in like a week because it's still too fuzzy.") Awesome. So washing, head massaging, nice smelling shampoos etc. ensue and we sit back down for the cut. Brie spent a few minutes with scissors and then asked me if it was ok to switch to a razor. I said of course, my old hair dresser in Nashville (who I miss with all my heart every time I have to get a hair cut somewhere else) used a razor every time. She says she always asks because some people have had bad experiences and try to avoid it. Nice. Finally we reach the styling point. She already asked what kind of products I like to use and so finds something similar from their arsenal but.. and this may have been my favorite part.. she just used a tiny bit and then sort of just let the style do itself. I like hair product as much as the next person, but almost every stylist I've ever seen has just used WAY too much gunk at the end of the cut. I end up walking out of the salon and wanting to go home to wash my hair immediately to get everything out. Not so here. I walked all the way home and when I took another look in the non-salon mirror, it looked exactly the way I would have done it myself. Amazing! Apparently they're moving a few doors down later in the month to expand the place. I can't wait to see the new larger space when I get my hair cut again in September(ish).

text: Yes, there will be a line. Yes, you'll sit at mix-and-match tables. And yes, you'll have to deal with the vagaries of a parking lot shared with a Rite Aid. There's no better place for breakfast, anywhere. Ming's pancakes are remarkable -- moist, buttery, and flavorful beyond imagining. Ming uses only the freshest of ingredients and keeps a watchful eye over her small but prodigious galley-style kitchen (which runs like clockwork) and table servers who are young, but skilled. Everyone works together to keep things moving. Ming's coffee is the best French Roast I've ever tasted -- and I'm not a fan of dark roasted coffees, especially in the morning. It's hard to know if all of her coffees are the product of a hand-press, but that's how every cup tastes. Never had a single cup delivered to our table which tasted stale, overbrewed or bitter. My wife loves Ming's teas, which are prepared to perfection. So, take a ride to Drexel Hill and enjoy breakfast at Ming's. You'll be delighted.

text: My husband and I decided that this is a great place for happy hour, but not necessarily a great dining experience. I would give Zing 3+ stars for tasty, creative food, but 2 stars because of the slow, apathetic service. We have eaten here a couple of times, and had similar experiences, so I don't think it was a fluke. It took several minutes after being seated for our waitress to take our drink order, and several more to bring the first round of drinks (including water). At least we had plenty of time to peruse the menu, so we ordered everything at once. Food came out quickly, and was presented by one of the chefs. I think our waitress came by only once after the food came out, and didn't ask if we were enjoying the food. The group at the next table also had bad service - they ordered more wine, and when it didn't come for over 20 minutes, they canceled the order, which seemed to make the waiter a bit mad. The food is innovative, but I think the dishes could use a bit of editing and work on execution. The fish tacos are the best in the city, with a crispy fried shell, stuffed with mahi mahi and topped with cilantro pesto. The risotto balls are a great concept, but were way too mushy inside. The shrimp and calamari both were perfectly cooked and served with a nice spicy sauce. The restaurant is located on the second-floor of an old building on the corner of Indiana Ave. & West St, which is a bit isolated from downtown. The decor inside is very modern and chic, and the balcony has a great view of the city. Zing serves its purpose for groups to leisurely enjoy cocktails and share small plates.

text: We ordered Fancy Fortune Cookies for our wedding and they were a big hit! Since our wedding colors were orange, blue and brown, we ordered the flavored cookies in orange, blueberry and chocolate. We also ordered coconut. For our "cake cutting," we ordered a giant cookie dipped in chocolate with fall-inspired colored sprinkles. The minimum number of cookies per custom order is 50. We ended up with 250 cookies and 105 guests, so there were a bunch leftover. My husband and I tried them before the wedding (and of course, we had our share after!) and they were delicious!! The blueberry tastes like blueberry waffles. Since we got custom fortunes, the cookies were all baked to order and they tasted fresh and delicious. The giant cookie was tasty, too! Just enough chocolate. My husband and I fed each other pieces and then our guests went to town on the remaining shards. Everything arrived in tip top condition. It also all arrived before my requested delivery date. When you place your order, they ask for a desired delivery date. The only minor issue I had was the custom fortune process. We had a quote from e.e. cummings on one and I typed it in exactly as I wanted it to print but they capitalized the letters. I should have specified in the Special Instructions section, but it might be helpful if they had a fortune proofing process before printing. I would definitely order from FFC again and highly recommend them for your event! Thank you for helping to make our wedding fun and special!!

text: "Meh" is really the best word to describe this place. Actually, no, the best way to describe it would be to get all grandiose and let William Shakespeare do it. I think these lines from "Much Ado About Nothing" sum up my feelings pretty well: BENEDICK. "Why, i' faith, methinks she's too low for a high praise, too brown for a fair praise, and too little for a great praise; only this commendation I can afford her, that were she other than she is, she were unhandsome, and being no other but as she is, I do not like her." Old Pueblo Grill is not an awful place, by any stretch of the imagination. It just doesn't really have anything by which it can commend itself. Thus, I would classify it as both totally innocuous and thoroughly unremarkable. It is the go-to, post-work watering hole of choice for my coworkers, due to its proximity to our workplace, so we will often find ourselves there on a Friday afternoon (as we did today). That said, if there was something nearby with more character, better service, or a more interesting menu, we would likely go there in a heartbeat. The decor feels a bit like the southwestern Holiday Inn that time forgot. Whenever I sit down in there, I constantly have to remind myself that I'm not actually hanging out in a hotel lobby. The walls have the standard, yet muted "holy shit, the desert sunset threw up on me" look to them, and the bar looks like it was designed by someone who owned a lot of bolo ties. The service is generally OK. Most of the waitstaff seems pleasant enough, but they sometimes seem annoyed at the idea of having to wait on a group of more than four people. They also seem chronically overwhelmed, even when the place is basically empty (as it seems to be on many afternoons). As others have written, the food is standard southwestern-influenced American fare. Our group usually orders the appetizers when we go, which consist of things like "Rattlesnake Eggs" (bacon-wrapped, cheese-stuffed jalapenos), various enormous quesadillas, and fried calamari (which always smells like death and looks almost as bad). I have one coworker who swears by the jalapeno concoction, but it just looks like a fried heart attack to me. The rest of the lunch menu is an uninspired assortment of overpriced salads and wraps with cutesy southwestern names. The dinner menu is marginally more interesting and contains some semi-fresh takes on old standards, like steak and salmon. Generally, though, the dinner food is significantly overcooked, which may have something to do with average age of the dinner clientele. Most seem to be in their 60s and 70s. I'll say this about the food, I have never tasted anything that was out-and-out bad, per se, but I've also never had anything that made me say, "Great googly moogly, I simply must have that again." The salsa is harmless and fresh, if flavorless, the salads are a touch on the limp side, and the wraps are OK, but they're nothing you couldn't just make in five minutes at home. For what you get, the food prices are pretty whack. Salads are in the $10-$12 range, and I think there is one app. on the menu for under $10. And that's the lunch menu. Frankly, the dinner menu has 4-star prices for 2-star food. On the boozy side, alcohol prices are par for the course and are nothing to either cry bloody murder or write home about. While we're talking booze, the beer selection is fine, if a bit tepid in the inspiration department. At least they don't limit themselves to Bud Light and Banquet Beer. There's usually Kilt Lifter, Fat Tire, and a rotating microbrew on tap. Mixed drinks are also on the strong side, which is pretty nice. A well-liquor vodka martini ran me $4.50 and was sufficiently alcoholic to the point that the rattlesnake eggs started to look kind of tasty. It wasn't brilliantly mixed, but it was fine. Old Pueblo Grill is a mixed bag, indeed. Too low for a high praise, to high for a low praise, too middle-of-the-road to be considered interesting, too nontoxic to be considered Lucky Wishbone. If it were demolished tomorrow, I likely wouldn't miss it. At the same time, though, I wouldn't slip the wrecking crew a Benjamin to "speed up the job and put some stank on it." Take of that what you will.

text: I debated whether or not to write this review, as I haven't actually eaten the food here - but after some thought - it was solely due to the service and attitude of the staff that we did not. Our friends had heard about Nitally's through some of those *other* review sites, and suggested we go there for a birthday dinner. Our plans had been made a few weeks ago, before Nitally's was listed as one of Tampa's Bests in a local newspaper. Our group of 5 arrived a little after 6pm on a Saturday night. The restaurant looks pretty small from the outside, and the red curtains in the windows remind me less of a restaurant and more of a sex shop. Opening the door, the place was smaller than we could have imagined. If you imagined a "hole in the wall" restaurant - this place would be the size of a corner in that hole in the wall. There were six or seven tables total - with two of them put together in the middle with a "reserved" sign on them. Unfortunately, they were not reserved for us. I stood in the doorway while one of our group spoke to a waitress about the table situation. It was going to be 20-25 minutes until an inside table would be available. We could, however, choose to eat outside. We decided we wanted to eat inside, but we would sit outside and enjoy some drinks while we waited. She brought some menus out and we looked over them for a few minutes to decide on our drinks. When she came back to take our orders, we found out that they were out of half the beers or flavors we wanted. We ended up with some various beers, wines and boba teas. The beer and wine were fine, but those who got the boba teas complained about the tapioca being very gummy. To top it off, they were served with regular straws - not ones wide enough to accommodate the balls. After being served our drinks, we were ignored for over an hour. Not once did the waitress come out to see if we wanted refills or if we had changed our minds about eating outside instead of waiting. After over an hour, our fearless leader went in to see what was going on as we could see an empty table from where we were sitting. There was a table for four open - but they weren't allowed to pull up an extra chair or combine the table with another due to issues with the fire marshall. I guess he also mentioned that we were being eaten alive by mosquitos. A minute or so after he returned, an employee came out with a fan and set it to blow towards us and went back inside. He came back out a few minutes later to ask if it had helped. It had not. He reiterated the issue with the combined tables - and offered an alternative: they had two tables that they could not combine - but we could split up our group and sit separately. WHAT? At that point, we decided we would go elsewhere. I'm torn now. The menu looked really interesting, and I'd really like to try their food - but their service and attitude makes me want to stay away. If you go, get take out or make reservations in advance.

text: The story of Cabana is a sad one for me. We were like college sweethearts who grew apart but denied it for a few awkward, painful months. My girlfriends and I used to take advantage of Wednesday martini specials for a dressy girls' evening out. The white bean hummus was (and is) spectacular. The waitresses were friendly and knowledgeable. The service and clientele changed drastically though and I no longer feel the same level of comfort. The music was the first change. I was told by one of the cocktail waitresses they stopped playing rap and other similar genres because they wanted a change in clientele. I gave them the benefit of the doubt by assuming they meant a change to the older, sleeker set which began filing in soon after. The drink prices went up slightly. The whole fee began to slowly change. I was still willing to forgive and adapt until one fateful day when the bartender yelled at us over my friend's $10 tab. My friend had put the money on the counter on top of his receipt. It had disappeared. Mysterious and disappointing sure, but we were treated as though we were trying to scam her even though the other three of us had already paid our more expensive tabs. "You can't just place cash on the bar," she said. Really? Because you can at every other bar ever. When the senior bartender approached we assumed it would be to calm her and remind her that customers, especially regulars, should be treated with respect. He did not. By then it had become a bit of a scene and other customers around us were making the "Are they serious?" eye contact with us. By the time a third employee joined and still refused to listen to reason we left. It's just one story, but to me it explains the impersonal effects of their attempt to re-market their restaurant. Frankly, even if we had been trying to stiff them, is it worth losing four customers over $10?
