text: Abstract: Nice Modern Football Stadium, with great viewlines, modern amenities, and passionate fans. ------------------------------------------- Time to yelp - Eagles season ticket holder since the Vet. Long time Birds fan (first game at age 13, 1972). Easy parking if you are coming from the north on 95 the Naval Yard Lot is easy on/off, but its a bit of a hike to the Linc. Game day parking is pricey ($15-$20). Tailgating is allowed but only in specific lots around the Linc. If in doubt, ask the attedent and look for the porta-johns. Check the Eagles website for more details. Public consumption of alcohol is sometimes policed. Dump the beer in a big plastic cup just in case. If you have some cash, arrive early and check out the "Head House Plaza" in the front of the stadium. The 100,000 square foot plaza features a giant video screen, entertainment, food and beverages, a team store, the Miller Lite Tailgate Zone, Touchdown Club and the Sovereign Bank Interactive Zone featuring an array of games and entertainment options for kids and adults alike. I cannot remember the name of the food stand (in front of the team store) that has an excellent pork sandwhich and Prima Pils beers on tap. I also like Fat Jack's BBQ. Outside of tailgating/HeadHouse Plaza or McFaddens at the baseball park there are zero other places to eat/drink outside the stadium. Once inside - look for the Chickies and Pete's (a Philly institution) - they feature Crab Fries and some nice spicy Chicken Fingers. Big Modern stadium with nice views. I sit in the upper deck, so its also a hike (up the sometimes swaying ramps) to get there. Greg P. finds us a "bowl full of A-Holes" and as a long time Eagles fan I'd have to agree that 10% of my fellow fans might just be that. Many fans avoid the Head House Plaza and drink to excess in the lots before the game. Eagles fans are high energy as compared to the 70 year old Giants fans (from the Yale Bowl Days) that snooze during most Giants games. Note to fans of the visiting team: I wouldn't wear a Red Sox hat to Yankees stadium - please don't wear your Packers/Giants/etc Jersey to the Linc. The boorish 10% will make your life miserable. It may not be "right" - but its a Philly thing. Its become more civil then the Vet but barely. At least they don't need the in-house courtroom any more (like they used to have at Vet Stadium!) Kimberly H writes "For the men: apparently there are only stalls and no urinals. Just an FYI...". This is partially correct. The old Vet had SERIOUS problems with the quantity of the ladies rooms (hour waits were common.) so they overbuilt the ladies rooms at the Linc. They converted a couple Ladies rooms to Mens Rooms (which is disconcerting as you go in to see only stalls!) Also, if you look around you can get good beer. Prima Pils are often available, and sometimes upstairs near my seats they will have Red Hook ESB on tap.

text: Being a pure Asian up in Caucasian Santa Barbara, I can confidently say that I've experienced better shabu shabu. Let's cut service and ambiance to the side, because Kai Shabu Shabu has typical Japanese restaurant service, which is in this case is - good, attentive service.Expected, and delivered well. Don't get me wrong - service was not a problem here. The waiter and waitress on duty were friendly and quick. I took a trip to the restroom too (I really had to go, not just for review purposes) and it wasn't dirty, as another Yelper reported. The restaurant in general seemed fairly clean. I guess they upped the cleaning since then? Well on to the shabu - like with all shabu places - comes with a choice of meat, and then you are given a plate of vegetables. Along with it a bowl of rice. What's lacking the most here is that you're not even given a soup base - just plain boiling water. How sad. Also, sauce only consists of that soy sauce like sauce (sorry, can't remember the name. I think it's sukiyaki sauce?) and the peanut ponzu sauce. You have shaved onions, minced radish, and minced garlic to add to the sauces, but that's it. I feel I've been to other shabu places that had a lot more mixing variety to their sauces - plus, the sauces offered at Kai Shabu Shabu aren't very flavorful. I had a large beef order, and the beef was okay. Nothing wrong with it. The overall food was good, but honestly the lack of soup base and somewhat blandness of the sauces made this visit non-3 star for me. Of course, I know I probably have to take into account that I'm from the San Gabriel Valley, where there are tons of shabu places and Asianess, and this probably the only location in Santa Barbara. So maybe I'm being too picky from my years of shabu eating (mind you, which started since I was a small kid). However, judging from the overall rating of this place, I'm guessing a majority of people aren't feeling this place. However because this seems to be the only shabu place in SB, and the fact that my meal wasn't necessarily bad or anything, I would say that you could definitely come here, as I personally think shabu shabu is a GREAT dining experience. It's tasty and supposedly healthy (I think maybe that's why there was no soup base here? I overheard the waiter working explaining to a pair of first timers that shabu is supposedly quite healthy). For me though, I'd definitely wait till I head home to LA on the weekends so I have my fill of shabu.

text: The Langhorne Hotel Tavern & Restaurant, is located in a beautiful and historic town. Victorian houses have been kept in pristine condition and painted in every color of the rainbow. Originally a log and stone building, built around 1700, this hotel has gone through many architectural changes and ownership. It was originally a "House of Entertainment" with a very large tavern. In 1905 the new owner turned it into a Country Inn. Travelers from Philadelphia would stop for meals on their trips to New York. Stagecoaches full of families, would come from all over just to dine here. In the hotel yard, there was a large livery stable with stalls for horses, a two story carriage house that was used to store wagons, carriages, and sleighs when not in use. The langhorne Hotel was transformed during WW1, prohibition, WW11 and the great depression. During WW11, the US government approached George G. Ehrlen, who had purchased the Hotel in 1905 and offered subsequent housing, so the building could be turned into five apartments for workers in local war plants. Ruth, the daughter of Mr.Ehrlen, is still alive and living in the house next door, She has many tales to tell and pictures to show. After the war the building was returned to the owner and remained empty until it was sold, once again. They renovated the first floor and resumed business. During one of the many renovations to the building, Ruth Irwin was able to salvage one of the original fireplace mantels which she still has in her present home. The hotel was sold in 1972, to the present owners, who maintain residency there and run the family owned business. Knowing they had a reservation for a party of twenty five, they had one server on, the owner came out and asked her if she needed him to call in another server, she said no, where he should have just taken the lead and called in more help. She was friendly, but running around like a chicken with her head cut off. She was also running the register and had her drawer full of money on the counter. I had to finally get up to get our menus and informed her that the cash drawer was out. The bartender came out to bus our table, told her she had a table in the tavern and wanted to know if she could pick it up. First the server said no, my head swung around and then she said, you go ahead and take it. The bar is large and the tavern seats quite a few people. Dimly lit, with a lot of old dark wood, beautiful fireplaces and down to earth friendly servers. The owner makes his presence known and will chat with you, for as long as you want. The entrance way has two large wooden booths, which have to be antiques and the main dining room, which was added on, is quite modern. The food... We used to dine here, years ago and we really did enjoy the food, however our recent visit here left us bewildered. We were not at all pleased with the quality, flavors or presentation. Maybe we ordered the wrong things and we did not complain, but I can not foresee rushing back there again. From the list of seventeen appetizers, hubby ordered the very small breaded clams casino, which were the best part of our entire meal. I had the crab imperial stuffed mushrooms, which had a lot of breading and they were just okay. We shared a huge Caesar salad, with the dark green outside leaves, they were lifeless. No anchovies were available for this un-crisp salad and powdered Parmesan topped it. The dressing was more like a ranch, with no hint of lemon or anchovy paste. Their side offerings leave a lot to be desired and are very old school. It is either fries, baked potato, a veggie melody, applesauce, jarred beets or cottage cheese. They have eighteen seafood entrees, nine veal dishes, three steaks, many chicken entrees, twenty seven different sandwiches and many choices of pasta. It was lunch time and we were hungry, hubby ordered the spaghetti with grilled sausages. He made it a point to ensure it was spaghetti and not linguine, he is so picky. They brought him super over cooked, to the point of mush linguine. He had them wrap it, even though he ended up pitching it. I ordered the Buffalo Chicken cheesesteak. Words can not justify the disaster of this sandwich. I like heat, but this was blazing hell, I love blue cheese, but not in a runny disgusting looking sauce. The real turn off was the chicken, it almost looked like someone had chewed it, spit it out and put it on the roll. They did not, but that was the consistency of the poultry. I had them box it, I took it home and tossed it out. Entertain yourselves here with a drink, reading the history of the Langhorne Hotel, from the place mats in front of you, enjoy the fireplace and a few apps. Maybe I should have tried the fried cod and chips, the fries were good. This Hotel has a wonderful past, but I fear for it's future, unless they hire a good cook.

text: This is just our personal experience based on our circumstances. From talking with other parents, I know that others have had different experiences. We signed our son up for the older babies/young toddlers' swim class. We had done the low-key class at the YMCA previously. We went to the classes that were held in the swimming pool of a retirement home. The school is the exclusive user of this pool at night. The pool itself was very very busy. While the class was going on in one section of the pool there were numerous private lessons with older children and instructors going on, as well as their parents hanging out around the pool. This wouldn't be too bad, but I think that the siblings or kids waiting for their lessons that hang out around the pool ramp were the biggest problem. I'd be walking my son down and 7-year-olds would be doing headstands or swimming beside us. It made it harder to enter the pool. Secondly, the amount of noise in that small pool did not make for a calm, peaceful environment. Third, there were so many toys just floating around the pool. I don't know why there were so many toys there. The pool edges were covered in toys - many of them those that didn't seem to be "pool toys" like stuffed animals. Maybe other kids are okay with that much stimulation, but my kid isn't. The class itself (babies/parents) was pretty large for the space. The impact of this was both that one didn't get as much one-on-one interaction as perhaps you'd hope and that there wasn't a lot of room to move. The range of abilities and ages was pretty wide. There were 3-year-olds that were nearly swimming on their own in with not-yet-walking babies. I realize that this is more due to the scheduling than preference of the school (you can't force people to do a Wednesday or a Monday if they don't want to), but it was a bit tougher. My son was not doing well in the class and while Wendy gave helpful suggestions for getting him more comfortable in the water (and I totally trust her opinion on this), they didn't jive with our parenting philosophy. We aren't believers in letting our son (at that time he was about a year old) cry through something that he isn't enjoying. Wendy could have totally been right that letting him cry through it could have worked, but I wasn't okay with it. And finally, when it came time to renew, I felt a lot of personal pressure from Wendy via phone and email to continue with the class. It was not working for us because our son wasn't happy, and we were going to be traveling extensively during the next class period, so signing up to take only a portion of classes wouldn't work for us. We also were limited as to what classes we could take because we were commuting from 40 minutes away. Although I clearly presented these issues to Wendy, she kept pressuring me to sign him up again. (And I have heard from other parents about this pressure.) I know that this is her business, but the pressure left a bad taste in my mouth. Business-wise, Wendy's school is very organized. The billing, the sign-ups, the class schedules, the listings -- while few are electronic (although some are), all are done very professionally. She has a ton of staff, all easily recognizable in their uniforms, mostly polite high school and college students. You're not likely to encounter issues on that side of things. All-in-all, if you are interested in your child swimming seriously (swim team or whatever), Wendy's school is a GREAT choice for you. Her instruction is good, she runs her business professionally, and there are a lot of options as a kid grows. If you are more like us, looking for a fun activity for parent-baby bonding that also helps baby get more comfortable in the water, Wendy's class is probably not for you. We had a good experience at the YMCA with a more relaxed class.
label: NEG

Now to the sushi...I had the Alaska Roll (Salmon and avacado) and the fish was so fresh and both ingredients were of a generous size. Usually they skimp on something at most places. The spicy tuna roll was alright, but I think I should have gotten my favorite, the Unagi (eel/avacado) roll. It actually comes with cucumber but I prefer avacado. Anyway, I was going to make that my 3rd roll, but I was too full to order it haha. All I have to say is....I will DEFINITELY go back and even the kids liked the place. This is a good place for a nice date, the atmosphere is classy and crisp, but the biggest table was a 6 seater in the center of the room, which is where we sat. The Cobblestone Grill has a patio, where you can enjoy a drink, dinner and dessert while listening to live music under the stars. Looking for ideas on what to eat? Try the quiche of the day, always a popular and yummy choice. If you don't like quiche, there's plenty of amazing dishes on this menu ... from crab cakes to portabella mushrooms (two more of my faves). Those are all on the lunch menu ... along with my fave at dinner, thai shrimp linguini. This dish will tempt the tastebuds and make it very difficult to decide! Looking for dessert? You seriously could pick any and not go wrong, but I suggest gelato or cheesecake. Or both.

I got there at 1:30 and ordered 10 wings and a beer. My beer came 20 minutes later. My wings never came because I got tired of waiting for them after two hours and canceled my order. On several occasions, when I ordered beer, they didn't give me a draft, but a bottle, and said they were going to charge me the same price as a "gift". I didn't bother arguing the fact that a pint glass holds more than a bottle because I was trying to fill my belly with beer since I didn't get the food I had ordered. I asked to speak to the manager before leaving to give him my thoughts. He said it was because a cook was out. text: I made my family to go there after reading reviews on Yelp. They were not very hungry in the first place and not impressed by the way the restaurant looked. Should have known better, because she kept eating everything she could reach! So much to say about the food that kids cannot stop eating! I was the only one excited about the place at the beginning, but by the end of the meal EVERYONE was in great mood. Even pre-teen got nice and happy, and picky eater ate every single bit we put on her plate - 3 times. We ordered Salt and Pepper Tofu, Green and Black Beans Chicken, 2 kinds of soups ( Seaweed one was the best), XO Grouper, Wine Chicken and Orange chicken. They don't bring each plate to the person who ordered it, they rather put all of them in the middle of the table and provide empty plates in front of everyone, so that, using the large spoons provided, each can put any amount of anything on his or her own plate. So, pretty much everything is served the way appetizers are normally served in American restaurants. Note, that portions are very large. Make sure you check the specials board located by the register - those offers are not even on the menu. We ordered our Green and Black Beans Chicken from it and my husband said that this is something he is going to order every time he comes here from now on. The service was great, I don't know why so many people commented about how poor it is. I prepared for the worst in that department, but was surprised to realize that it;s quite the contrary. Everyone was very attentive, quick and friendly. They didn't even mind the baby who was loud and messy, not even the gloomy pre-teen, they smiled to both of them and tried to entertain them (successfully). The waitress didn't even hesitate when the 5-year old was placing an order and told her that the only things she wanted were macaroni n' cheese or chicken nuggets. She replied with an offer of orange chicken nuggets and was granted a consent. Orange chicken turned out to be beautiful and delicious and our daughter said this is the only kind of chicken nuggets she wants to eat from now on. No dessert on the menu, but if you ask, the will provide one. We, however, chose the boba tea in the tea room right next to this restaurant. Our bill turned out to be little more then $50 and we felt like leaving a good tip. Will definitely be back

I like the selection of bread you can choose from for your sandwich. I almost always choose the foccacia bread. Their salads also something I enjoy. Like their sandwiches, fresh flavorful ingredients are always used. The English Stilton With Asian Pear Walnut salad, an odd-sounding combination, is full of flavor with the slight sweetness of the pear balancing the sharp flavor of the Stilton cheese. Most salads and sandwiches start at $8 making this restaurant a bit pricey but once the quality of ingredients is considered the price is rather reasonable. They also have a nice selection of gourmet sodas. Inside and outside seating is available. Their meals are well packaged for take out.

text: "What's your favorite restaurant?" If you're a loudmouth, always-hungry type like me (and most opinionated yelpers!), you get this question all the time. I'm more of a top-five, what's-the-context type of girl, coyly hedging my bets to dodge this sticky question. But for almost any occasion, Mémé takes my top spot. The food is always simply prepared -- rustic, even -- giving the impeccable ingredients a chance to really shine. Technique is king to chef David Katz, who once called my boyfriend and I "warriors" when we requested even more courses after eating what most non-mutant humans would consider a normal meal. The menu changes all the time, so go with the seasonal flow here. One of my staples is the smoked salmon flatbread -- sounds easy, blows your head off when you take that first smoky, saline, chaud-froid bite. Desserts are just as expertly prepared -- any sort of upmarket pudding/custard jawn will finish you off with style (creme brulee, panna cotta, budino, you get where I'm going here.) Last but not least, service is friendly, elegant and uber-professional. They care.

text: Like pizza? But sometimes want an authentic Italian dish? Then run, don't walk, to Caln Pizza. I grew up in North Jersey, just outside New York. I went to school in the Trenton area, famous for its Chambersburg Italian Restaurant Row. I know pizza. And this is some of the best around - especially in the 'burbs. Caln Pizza could hold its own in a city; it's a suburban standout. The pizza selections run from a nice, thin Neapolitan to traditionally thick and tasty Sicilian and tomato pie. Toppings are diverse and delicious - basically, you name it, the guys at Caln Pizza will make it. The comfortable shop in Caln Village Shopping Center offers other must-have casual fare: strombolis, calzones, cheesesteaks, hoagies, char-broiled sandwiches, etc. What sets Caln Pizza apart are the specials. The co-owner and head chef makes pretty much everything from scratch, right down to the sauce (gravy, if you're from the old country). A secret sauce, I might add ... I'm on a first-name basis, and I can't wiggle the ingredients out of him! Homemade is the rule at Caln Pizza. This means seafood, chicken, beef, veal and other not-so-pizza-shop entrees are out of this world. I have to say it ... it's like mamma and nana used to make! My favorite quick meal: tomato pie thick slice, regular slice and a small salad. My husband's favorite quick meal: the daily special. Seriously. He gets it almost every time! I highly recommend this friendly place for a yummy bite to eat.
label: POS

text: Are you prepared for a saga? Jammy (pronounced Jamie) at the Jewelry Exchange has been absolutely wonderful. My fiancee and I ventured over here in search of a wedding band that would fit against my engagement ring (the ring has a marquise ruby with a mounting that rests against my finger, not set up above the ring like a solitaire). We had just been to Jared, where a salesperson recommended that I get a plain white gold band and cut a notch out of it to fit. I asked Jammy if that was something they could do, and upon consulting with their jeweler, she regretfully informed me that doing so would weaken the integrity of the band & as such they wouldn't do it. (-1 for Jared, seriously.) I had seen a solitaire-and-enhancer set at a jewelry store in the Westshore Plaza & asked Jammy if they had anything like that there. No, but they did have other wedding sets. (I was already considering getting a new set altogether & moving my ruby over, or maybe getting a new ruby.) & she showed me a mounting with 2 small marquise diamonds on the engagement ring and 3 diamonds on the wedding band, that had a unique shape to it, & I absolutely fell in love. But it was sparklier than what I had had in mind, & I said so, so she recommended that I think about it, look around, & come back later to see the new styles that they get in each week. I couldn't get the ring out of my head, though, & we returned twice in 2 weeks & I had eyes for only that one. By now, though, I'd decided that I did indeed want a new ruby with a deeper red for my new ring, but the Jewelry Exchange doesn't sell loose rubies. So I looked online and did a little bit of calling around, but I only found one website that sells loose marquise rubies (I was absolutely dead-set on a marquise) & they were a little more expensive than what I had in mind. When, on Saturday (our 6 year anniversary), my fiancee and I went into the Jewelry Exchange to buy the rings, I asked Jammy if she knew where I could go to get a loose ruby. Why, they can order one from the home office for me! She took down my info, measured the ruby in my current ring, & promised to call with some quotes. Sure enough, Monday afternoon she called to tell me what they had. It still sounded a *little* bit high, so I asked her to check one size smaller and call me back. I'm expecting to hear from her today or tomorrow about that. I've reconsidered & I think I do want to get the one she quoted, but I'll see what she says about one size smaller first. So far my experience with the Jewelry Exchange has been FABULOUS. I felt no pressure to buy at any time, & Jammy really seemed to want to help me find the perfect ring. Since we bought them, I feel like all I want to do is stare at my new rings & I can't wait till there's a ruby nestled in there! I'll be sure to put up a picture & update my review as soon as that's done. 5 stars for a WONDERFUL establishment -- with great staff & great prices!!

There you have it, as every taste is reached: hot, cold, spicy, sweet, salty, creamy, crunchy. Although the seating is a modest arrangement, the portions definately aren't! text: Okay, so I know I'm not going to make any friends with this review, but hear me out before you judge. Blueberry Hill is a St. Louis landmark. Period. Perhaps it's to catch a glimpse of Chuck Berry, to look at the display cases of collectible knick-knacks, or perhaps it's just because they heard so much about it they must see for themselves. Whatever the reason, it doesn't matter what I say about Blueberry Hill. People, for some reason, love it, and keep telling their friends about it. So here is my list of complaints: 1) Why don't you hire someone who cares about actually being a waiter/waitress? Meaning, someone who will actually be attentive and cordial to the table. 2) Why don't you put some decent (not out of a box) vegetarian dishes on your menu? 3) Why don't you close the place down for a week and clean it up? I hate looking at layers and layers of dust when I eat. If you must go to Blueberry Hill, here are a few things that are safe to order: Mac n' cheese, burgers, and onion soup. Stay far away from the rest of the menu; I've seen inside their kitchen.

text: This was my second tour of the cemetary in 5 years and Haunted History again came up short when compared to my previous visit tour company. Before I continue this review I should state that my expectation from tour guides is that they will provide historical and relational facts about the tour subject. Tours should not be a soapbox for individual opinion and heresay. If you like the tour guide to give their opinion you may not agree with my assessment of Ernie, our guide on HH's Cemetary tour. Interesting that Ernie is singled out as a great tour guide because he was our guide who ultimately must be accountable for the failure of value of our tour. He was very jaded and espoused his sarcasim and negative opinions about New Orleans leaders and organizations in the guise of humor throughout the entire tour. Whereas he led everyone to believe he was an expert on NO history, he really gave no unique information to separate him from any other guide who has conducted daily tours for a couple of years. For example, when I asked if any famous musicians were lain to rest in St. Louis #1 he told me yes, but none I would know. That was his brief answer and he offered no name. How would he know the musicians I would know? Unfortunately, Ernie's negativity, aloof nature and dry mannerism are an unnecessary distraction that permeate his entire tour and left me disappointed. Bottomline I would recommend before you take a cemetary tour, go ahead and walk the cemetary with a guide book and you will likely receive as much if not more information. There is a lot of information about theives and concern in the cemetaries but if you go during the day, you can walk St. Louis #1 yourself and find Laveau's tomb yourself. When you read about her, you will actually realize she isn't as interesting as the tour industry of New Orleans wants you to think. Read about Louis Armstrong who is much more important in terms of music and social culture.

text: Started off a 7-bar pub crawl on Saturday at "The Mack". It was a little after 3 and none of us had eaten lunch in anticipation of the steak sandwich, which was vouched for by a Southampton native. With the spectacular storm brewing outside we prepared to hunker down for some pub grub and brews. Three ordered the steak sandwich and I went with the 1 lb "Man Burger" (I knew I'd score some of the steak from my petit bride). The burger was fantastic. If you've read my recent O'Connell's burger review you'll see I was none too fond of their offering. The Mack's burger blows O'Connell's burger away. Ironically, O'Connell's was just named the number 1 St Louis area burger according to the RFT. I challenge anyone to try them side by side and prefer O'Connell's flavorless bloodbath of ground-beef. Anyway, huge props for this massive, tasty cheeseburger, nicely priced at $7.50. That all said, I should have gone for the steak sammy, as was the original plan. From what I tasted of my lady's sandwich, it was the best cutlet of steak I've had in all of St Louis. Yes, it was better than anything I have tasted at Tucker's Place (and I've had a steak or ten there). Trimmed of fat and gristle, the 5 chunks of perfectly-seasoned steak served between two pieces of cheese garlic bread were a steak-lover's dream. At $9 for the sandwich and side, I'd challenge anyone to find a better or larger cut of steak in the land. I have had dozens of mediocre steak sandwiches in my day. You know the ones where you take a bite and the entire piece of steak comes off in your teeth as you try to bite through the sinew and gristle, then inevitably have to spit a chunk of it into a napkin because there's no way it's fitting down the gullet? None of that here. I would estimate that the total weight of the 5 chunks of steak after cooking to be around 16 oz (or more). This is a bargain by anyone's standards. Golden Tee on the widescreen. SilverStrike antiquated 2007 version. Nice side room for steel tip darts (5 boards). Friendly staff. Several flat screens. Bon appetit!

text: I boarded 2 of my dogs here once and was not happy. My one dog was 17 yrs old and I thought that being it was also a vet she would be in good hands. They put her in an outside run that was partly covered and they put my smaller pomerainian in a small cage in a room full of cats. I figured it would be ok as I was only leaving them there for two nights. WhenI dropped them off I told them my older dog might have to be tranquilized as she would chew on the cage and tear her mouth open in the past when she was boarded. I didn't think my pomerainian would have a problem as she slept in a cage at home. When I picked them up, my old dog had open cuts on both sides of her mouth that were infected and they had never ttranquilized her and when they brought out my pom, she had rectal bleeding from the stress of being boarded that they never noticed. I don't know how they could have missed the bleeding as it was all over her fur in her back end and blood was coming out AS SHE WALKED. So not only did I have to pay for having them boarded, but then I had to pay for medicine to treat them for the problems they came out with. They didn't however charge me for the vet exam. Not sure how long my pom was bleeding, could have started from the first day she was there. Needless to say I will never board a dog there again. text: Thousands of people riding their bikes all over the City of St. Louis! That kind of fun can't be beat. Here are a few tips: WEAR A HELMET. There's a ton of people on this ride who are not familiar with cycling etiquette and allow thoughts of mass bicycle crashes. I really didn't see any heinous crashes, but the potential is there. There are some cycling shops available to help you with your bike if it needs work. Helmets First, a non profit organization was also available to sell donated helmets to the lidless. I've heard this isn't all that rare in Philly but still 3) Location 4) Dependably very good food 5) Excellent mussels (although a little on the small side) with great sauce 6) Really excellent quality food for the price 7) Great atmosphere! The bad: 1) Weird service - they were so attentive that I actually felt like they were rushing us out (even though the place wasn't packed). I honestly started to feel like I had to guard my appetizer plate from being taken away from me! I don't think they should try and take the appetizer, especially a mussel plate, when there is still food on it. With that said, I believe they were well intentioned - I'd hate to see them sabotage their good intentions much longer. 2) The salmon dish was good but the salmon was slightly overcooked - not dry but not as flaky as I like. 3) Cash only 4) The fish special was $23.95 - a full $8 more than the fish item on the menu! Definitely ask the price before you order a special. Final word: Will definitely go back again for the great food, relaxed environment, and great BYO policy. Just hope the wait staff gets less pushy!

text: OOOOO-WWWEEE this place was a mess...Sadly, the best way i can describe the Saint Louis Hotel is that it reminded me of a once beautiful woman who was ridden hard and put away wet...on Bourbon Street..in the middle of summer. In other words, whether it be from post-Katrina damage, or overall poor maintenance, it did not age well. I booked my reservation as part of an air + hotel package deal on Bookit.com. For $52 dollars a night, my Deluxe King Room seemed like an awesome deal. I looked at their website to make sure it was decent, and from the photos, and list of amenities, it did not seem so bad. I was particularly intrigued by the lush tropical courtyard prominently featured in the website. So we cab it from the airport to hotel, and from the outside, it seemed like everything looked swell. We walked in the lobby at about 8pm and I noticed that the lobby was completely deserted and there was no one at the front desk. Waited a good 10 min. before someone made it from out the back office and checked us in. The guy checking us in was not very friendly, not very welcoming, and rushed through the check in process as if he had better things to be doing. As a seasoned traveler, i know that more often than not, hotels offer free upgrades if there is space and availability. I asked if there was any possibility of a room upgrade, and the guy gave me a look that would have been deserved if i had asked him to stick a pine cone up a certain orifice, and flat out said "NO". Did not check the computer or even offer to check, just directly said "No". When i politely brought this point to his attention, he gave me attitude and said that i was booked on a special rate. Whatever. I was hungry, tired, and wanted to get settled in, so i left it at that and checked in. We waited another 10 mi. in awkwardness till a porter cam for our bags. Our luggage was loaded onto a cart and we were unceremonously shown into a rickety elevator that smelled faintly of stale vomit and lemon pledge. Our porter took us all the way around the 3rd floor, before he remembered that our room was on the 2nd floor. Oookay... Get back in the elevator, and make our way to the 2nd floor. Instead of our room being in the actual Hotel building, we were taken out back and into another building that was once, in its past life, servant's quarters. I'm dead serious when i say, the hotel room i stayed in was a converted servant quarter. The porter left our bags in the front of the room, and left. We opened the room, and were dismayed to find a tiny room (about 12 x 15 sq ft) with a FULL sized bed, 2 pillows, an arimoire housing the TV. The closet was barely big enough for 2 people's luggage, and the bathroom was downright shabby with peeling wallpaper exposing mould underneath. So much for a Deluxe King room. Despite the 'deal' i got on the price, I still feel like i was misled or cheated. So here's the breakdown of the pros' & cons' +1 star- Location, Location, Location: it is right in the French Quarter, one block away from the madness of Bourbon and 5 brisk blocks from Jackson Square, and 2 blocks from Canal Street. If you plan on partying hard or want to be centrally located so you can drop your shopping bags off in between your French Quarter sprees, its location is ideal. There is a Chase bank (with the worlds loudest ATM) half a block away and most late night restaurants (not to mention the heaven sent Krystal Burger) are literally a stagger, skip, and stumble away. +1 star-- Central Courtyard. This is the only jewel in the St. Louis' crown. The open air courtyard was tented for the winter, but that did not detract from the lushness of the plants or the beauty of the fountain. There were private functions 3 of the 5 nights we stayed there, but during the day, many hotel patrons enjoyed their breakfasts and lunches in this charming and exotic setting. -1 star-- Service. Granted, I was not expecting Ritz Carlton like service, but overall, I was pretty disappointed about the staff, especially the front desk, who run this place. Its like they either forgot or just did not pay attention to Hospitality 101. The only nice employees we encountered were the dining room staff and the kind old man who does security at night. The only problem is, half the time, he's not at the security desk. -1 star- Housekeeping. Granted, i have slight OCD, but i really had issues with the housekeeping and overall maintainence of this place. Some examples are: on the first night, we called the front desk at about 7pm and asked for 2 extra pillows since there were only 2 on the bed. They said they would send them right up, but they never came. We had to ask again the next morning as we were leaving for breakfast. We came back 5 hrs. later, we found 2 pillows haphazardly flung on top of our still unmade bed. In addtion to the mouldy wallpaper in the bathroom, the showerhead was unscrewed and one of our towels had stains on it. yuck.

text: Last night, the Boy and I ventured down to the Philly Night Market in South Philly and like so many others, once we saw how long the lines were, we decided to find a restaurant to eat at instead, and just enjoy the ambiance. We've heard quite a bit about Izumi, and we're always on the lookout for GOOD sushi (not that many choices in this city), and since they were able to seat us right away at the bar, this seemed just perfect! Flash forward 2 hours and 40 minutes later, we'd consumed roughly 6oz of food apiece. The kitchen had botched our order 3 times; the only way we managed to get any food whatsoever was when our concerned waitress wandered over every 40+ minutes to cock her head to one side and muse "oh, did you not get your such-and-such yet? I'll go check!" Only to put the order back in the kitchen's queue, not at the front of the line, where it should have gone. I take full blame for not standing up for myself and pointing out how ridiculous their multiple errors were. I'm not complainer by nature, but this was beyond any mistake I've seen in a restaurant. At the end of our stay, when the waitress sheepishly informed us that our last dish was "still cooking....slowly. Do you want to just get your check?" I told her to just forget it. We then saw them pull a raw piece of meat out of the oven and throw it away. We would have been there for another 45 minutes, at least. What infuriated us the most was the lack of offering to take something off the check, let alone comp the whole dinner. Or at least bring over something as a "while you're waiting" apology. I don't feel as though the world owes something to me, but I do believe in restaurant etiquette. The restaurant was crowded, but there wasn't a line out the door - it was just "normal full". As the tables around us were efficiently fed and turned over, I resigned myself to leaving a 0% tip (NEVER did that before!) and promised to never darken their doorway again. I give this place one star for 2 reasons: 1.) Yelp doesn't let you give zero stars 2.) The food that they did give us (a hastily ordered salmon-and-avocado roll and a spicy tuna roll - not exactly what you go to a destination sushi place to eat - just to have something to chew on!) was actually pretty good. Thanks for a lot of nothing, Izumi. Maybe I'll come back the next time I have a 3+ hour car inspection waiting time.

text: Sallie Mae and I are really, really close. We've been friends for years. At first, Sallie was a giver. She gave, and she gave, and she gave. And in many ways, I think I took advantage of that. Then, all of a sudden, after years of this one-sided relationship, things turned around for us. Now she just takes, takes, and takes. So each month, I have a large sum of my income directly debited to Sallie. And she's content. You must be thinking: Why do you owe Sallie so much money? Was it your expensive schooling? Me: Why no. I had a full scholarship. You: Then why? Me: Because of the Red Sox, the torture that was my grad school program, and Pep Boys. Let me explain. When I was in undergrad, I spent my student loan money on Red Sox tickets. Lots of them. I went to at least a hundred games a year. I drank beer that Sallie gladly paid for. Bought t-shirts with players who soon left for other teams. And ate my fair share of steak tips. In grad school, I had to work 40 hours a week (for free) so I used student loans to pay for things like rent, food, gas, bills, etc. To offset my stress, I occasionally (nightly) splurged on going out to dinner and ate a large quantity of fast food in the front seat of my car. Then I had to purchase larger clothes...All with the kind support of Sallie Mae. And finally, my dad picked out a junker car for me, and I visited Pep Boys on a monthly basis for several years replacing probably every part of my car, several at a time, until she finally died a slow death in Boston several years later. Pep Boys employees knew me by name, often "suggested" I junk my car, gave me ads of cars that were on sale, drove me to and from school on occasion, and fixed my car each time. They also gave me great deals after finding out that Sallie was already accruing interest on the money I owed them. The few times when I bothered to get a second opinion, I was always given the same list of repairs from the other car repair shop, but a higher estimate somewhere else. So I stayed faithful to Pep Boys. Many thousands of dollars later, my car left Nashville, and somehow made it to San Diego, and then back to Boston. It died on Commonwealth Avenue, on our way to Anna's Taqueria. Though I never got a burrito that night, Pep Boys did ensure that I got close... And for that, I will always be thankful!

text: One of Indy's best Latin restaurants just moved downtown. I attended a preview of it yesterday, and all I can say is: Finally. A place for Texans like myself to feel down-home. What's new at this place is manifold, but my fav is the great big (and orange!) layout, which really allows the place's décor to shine: A loteria-flavored table upstairs reads "El Corazon," with a giant heart plastered across its shiny mosaic tiles. Rustic upstairs railing provides a novel frame for gazing on diners below. A private dining room centers on a crucified calavera piece. The layout is like no other in the city. And so is the food. Make no mistake: This isn't a straight-up interior Mexican restaurant. The place is famous for its margaritas and guacamole, but there's so much more to it. It's pan-Latin, with a range of options--from myriad ceviches to those kissed with sweet Caribbean touches. Back to those ceviches, 'cause this is a hot trend, the likes of which Indy has only seen at its uptown cousin's, Chicago. I tried a seared scallop concoction topped with jicama and a tangy/sweet red reduction that was as tasty as it was pretty. But my favorites have to be the traditional interpretation with shrimp, or the sashimi-style tuna with a chile de arbol dollop that conjures Sriracha sauce. So Latin 2.0!

text: I've been a fan of the King Buffet for years. If not for the food, for the fact that it's just fun to eat, there. They've got an awesome selection of dishes to choose from, a complete salad bar, and even a children's food bar for those who aren't quite into their parents' ideas of good eating and apt to go batshit the entire time Mom and Dad are trying to enjoy their meal. The food's alright. But, being a buffet, you know it's not going to be as one might expect a restaurant serving fresher entrees would be. It's no worry, though, as the staff is seen regularly ferrying hotpans full of goodies to replace the depleted and, as there's always a decent amount of people around, what's under those heatlamps doesn't stay there long. Usually. There's always that one item, that day, that's not as popular as its brethren and you're left kind of wondering. But I've never had a complaint to offer toward their quality. It's just a fact that buffets of any sort anywhere share, that they're simply not going to be serving food as fresh as a traditional eatery. Some people are more sensitive to that than others. I could eat an egg sandwich left on my kitchen counter at home for nine weeks and barely suffer a burp while somebody else might go into convulsions after eating a lukewarm fry that's been out of the oil for slightly better than fifteen minutes. As it is an all-you-can-eat buffet, feel free to sample what you feel may be of dubious quality before lumping an effing ton if it onto your plate, find something you like, take it to your table, enjoy, and get on with your life. Don't be a pussy - take a chance. And have a good time. One thing I should point out: you'll notice that the wait staff are always standing around the place at intervals like guards in a prison mess hall. Don't let this freak you out. Because of them, I have never been shanked yet while dining at the King Buffet, nor have I ever had to give up my pudding to the guy at the next table else he jumps me in the men's room, later, and makes me toss his salad for refusing. Oh. Lastly. Sometimes, they serve this dish with little octopi in it. If you've got a kid with you, it's always worth a laugh to dump some of that onto his or her plate. It's worth the crying and resultant therapy you - or your sister and brother-in-law - will be paying for, trust me.

text: Sometimes I think there a rule among Philly sandwich shops. The better they are, the less frequently they are allowed to be open. The 24 hour tourist traps are pretty bad, and at the other end of the spectrum, you have John's You pretty much have to live or work in South Philly to get a chance to go to John's, because they keep bankers hours. And when they say they close at 3, they mean 3 is when the bread is usually gone, so don't think you can sneak in a 2:40, I've been there late as they started surveying the line to figure out who would get the last roll. Despite a lot of praise from all corners, John's remains largely off the beaten path, with much longer lines at the other cheesesteak institutions. That being said, if you ever have a weekday off, you need to get here. Both the cheesesteaks and the roast pork sandwiches vie for the title of best in the city. The rolls are fantastic, lightly seeded with a good thick crust and a light but not spongy breadiness. The pork is perfectly seasoned and nicely juicy. As a bonus, most of the people in line are waiting for a cheesesteak, so you can jump to the front for a roast pork and other non grilled items. Definitely get the pork with sharp provolone and spinach, its really is a marriage made in heaven. The cheesesteaks are cooked to order on a big griddle. Unlike the assembly lines of Passyunk avenue, cheese whiz is verboten here, provolone is the cheese of choice, and they expertly melt it into the meat. Their menu has a good variety of cheesesteak offerings, including chicken cheesesteaks, but I prefer to keep to the classic. They also make cold hoagies, but the point is the hot sandwiches. Like any great steak shop, they have no indoor seating and limited outdoor seating. The building itself is on an island between some railroad tracks, the strip malls on Snyder ave, and an imposing factory. It makes a great place to grab lunch while shopping along Delaware ave, as it is right between the Target and the Ikea down there.

text: We had an amazing dinner here. I highly recommend getting the gigantic martini shaker to share with friends. The Lobster Mac N Cheese was divine. We were so happy we went the next day for brunch. Not so much of a brunch scene. Sort of bright and the food was solid but not amazing.

text: The yogurt is different from other yogurt places in town...creamier. It's a good thing. Sometimes I just get fruit; other times I go decadent with cornflakes and dulce de leche. I would give this place five stars, except that I DESPISE the stupid blue cups. The design, with very shallow, straight sides to the cup because the cup does double duty as two different sizes, means that you get about four berries per small serving. One really has to get one of the two larger sizes in order to get any discernable toppings to stick to one's yogurt. I swore I wouldn't return until they redesigned these idiotic cups that dictate skimpy topping quantities. But I haven't been able to stay away. (Hey, at least the cups are biodegradable.)
label: POS

text: This was the worst meal I have ever had in my life. I think this place is recommended for brunch which I unfortunately did not eat during this time. I went on a Friday night for dinner with three other people. I just ordered a side salad which was quite mediocre. The other three people in the party ordered crab au gratin, fried catfish, and penne pasta with shrimp. The crab au gratin was completely gross and consisted of a runny cheese sauce with no evidence of real potatoes and barely a trace of crab meat. The catfish was so dry and boring and the penne pasta was just smothered in cheese with popcorn shrimp. How can a place that charges so much for a dinner entree serve popcorn shrimp? The ambiance was awful as well. I felt like I stepped back in time and not in a good way. The place felt old and stuffy. I will never eat here again. By the way, there was only one other family there in the whole restaurant while we were there on a Friday night at 8PM!

text: OK, it has happened to everyone. You're already having a bad day, then something goes wrong with your car! Never fear - Polly's Service Center to the rescue. If your vehicle is really, really sick they have a towing service, which for a reasonable fee will come to you and tow in your car! This happened to me and the folks at Polly's could not have been more helpful. Native Nashvillians, the staff at Polly's explained to me that a mechanic would perform an inspection and call me with a "diagnosis" and estimate. True to their word, they called within one hour. The parts were ordered and my car was ready that afternoon. Their prices are very reasonable considering what you would pay at a dealership! When I was there I had just gotten my new Tennessee car tag, so the friendly mechanic offered to put it on for free! You can't argue with that!! The best thing about Polly's is that they really try to make you feel appreciated as a customer. They know all too well that having major car problems is the source of a great deal of stress, and they let you know they are fixing the problem as soon as possible. When it was time to change my spark plugs, a simple task compared to the engine trouble I had previously, there was no question where I was going for this routine care! Polly's is just as efficient at this simple task. When all is said and done, Polly's sends you on your way very relieved, and your wallet not too much lighter!

text: Loved the crowd and the vegetarian shepherd's pie. The shepherd's pie is the ultimate comfort food. I had mine with garlic and it was heavenly. It was even good microwaved a day or two later. The wine I had was very good as well. Our waitress was a doll. We loved the lemon meringue dessert she recommended. I will definitely be back! thank you Family Wash.

text: Met a friend for dinner here tonight with my wife. I was pretty surprised when we walked in - I was expecting a bar and grill atmosphere, not a higher end looking restaurant with nice finishes and some pretty cool art. Surprise number one, down. The food was the next surprise. It wasn't bar food. The entrees were actual, real, tasty entrees with well executed sides. Color me impressed. Yays: - The food was great. I had pork tenderloin, she had salmon, and our friend had a reuben. We were all impressed. - The soup may have been better than the food. I had the soup trio (what a brilliant idea - three small samples of soup that totaled about one bowl worth) and I could definitely go back for a bowl someday. - The bread was also darn tasty - Large cocktail menu, and a great wine list - The finishes and overall atmosphere were very pleasant. It was quite busy but not too loud. - The server was quick and came back several times to check on us. Just the right amount of visits. - They have both lunch and dinner portions of food. I had the lunch portion, and it was plenty. Nays: - My pork was a touch charred. I had to cut off a few overcooked bits. - The tea was yuck. I don't know if I've had such poor quality tea in my life.
label: POS

text: We went to Village Whiskey on a Friday night with some out of town friends who were dying to try it. I was warned about the potential for a big wait, so no surprise when were arrived at 8:15 and given a hour and a half wait time. Pleasantly surprised however, when they took both our name and number and were told we would be called when our table opened up. Spent a pleasant hour watching the Phillies game around the corner at Irish Pub until we were called that our table was ready. We were even seated at a table outside! Service was great - our server was very pleasant and gave us some great recommendations. I started with a Ginger Rogers, which though small, was really yummy. Later on we had Dogfish Head Festina Peche, which they had on tap. We knew we had to get the duck fat fries, and went for the Best of Philly winner - with cheddar sauce & short ribs. Akin to a religious experience in my opinion. Really excellent. The pickled artichokes were also a nice starter. Three of us had the Village Burger - nicely cooked, and juicy. One rebel ordered the Pulled Pork, which came with coleslaw and fried pickles. A BBQ snob, he gave it a solid 2 thumbs up. The rest of us were so jealous of the pickles we ordered 2 extra sides of them - crisp and not greasy! My only downside was the one, unisex bathroom, which ended up having quite a line. For a Garces restaurant this really surprised me.
label: POS

Kitchen K does better than most. The menu is interesting and sometimes changes, and there are some weird things served here that you won't find everywhere else. How often do you find bouillabaisse and pork chops on the same menu? The food is better than your chain restaurants but is typically slightly less satisfactory than other stand alone restaurants. One must admit that the atmosphere makes up for it, though. The design of the place is awesome and there's art to look at, not to mention the open kitchen you can spy on!

text: Alright so it has the appeal of being in the french quarter, and our drinks were very good but the rest left something serious to be desired. To start we had the spinach dip- which was good, nothing to write home about and as the dish goes it's pretty hard to screw up. For main courses she had the chicken- again good, but not very "cajun" flavored and certainly nothing special. I had the combination platter of jambalaya and a shrimp dish- both of which I would have given one star. The Jambalaya tasted like it had refried beans mixed into it and the shrimp in the other dish were small, tasted as if they had been frozen and cooked for too long and was only good after I added a lot of creole seasoning and salt and pepper. We also ordered a side of crawfish etouffee was horrible, pretty much inedible because of how fishy it was- I know fresh sea food, nothing, not even the most "fishy" tasting fish tastes that bad. Plus at $8 for a serving you'd expect something not only good, but more than a cup (literally that volume measurement) or less of it. It got 2 stars for atmosphere and the drinks...

text: DO NOT use this service. I called for a cab on the 4th of July and was told the wait would be 15 - 30 minutes, and to sit and wait on the curb (in a shady neighborhood mind you). After a half hour, I called back to check the status of my cab, only to be informed by dispatcher that I had only called 2-3 minutes earlier for a cab, which was NOT the case. The dispatcher then informed me that it would be an hour from the time I placed my call, so I hung up and waited that extra half hour. After waiting just over an hour total, I called back a THIRD time, to find out that a driver had not even been ASSIGNED to my pickup. Couch Tomato makes a mean pie, and they do it with a smile upon their faces to boot. text: I'm giving this place two stars for a few reasons. Our server was definitely lacking some brain cells for one. We ordered some cocktails off of their specialty drink list that weren't very good at all. They were horribly sour. I had the mai tai and my husband had the zombie. We got the calamari which was the best thing we had all night. It was cooked well and had a really good dipping sauce with it. Afterwards we decided to order the hot wings because there was a daily specials menu attached to the actual menu that stated that the specials are served all day and the wings were just 50 cents each. After ordering them, our waiter comes back after ten minutes saying that the specials menu wasn't valid afterall and that we could still have the wings if we wanted to pay full price for them. So it wasn't an issue of them being out of wings. I was really upset that they weren't willing to honor the price that we had ordered them at. We ordered the riblets instead and weren't impressed at all. They were tough and a little dry aside from the load of bbq sauce on them. It's a small restaurant that gets pretty noisy at peak dinner time, but I'll take lively over eerily silent any day.

text: One of the few shops in New Orleans in my brief visit that actually got me excited. The boutique is packed with wonderment and tons of fabulous finds. I only regret that I visited so near closing time. Hours of exploration can easily be found here. Some of my favorites included a sassy collection of feminist friendly books, silver compacts and cigarette cases, pretty purses, a small shrine to earrings, home decor, as well as a decent collection of cute I-would-actually-wear-this clothing.

She made up some excuse about why she couldn't turn it off and walked away without getting a drink order. It was so cold that I was shivering and I told my boyfriend we had to leave. I don't plan on ever going back here because clearly it is not meant to be.

text: I probably am being harsher than it actually is. Perhaps, i could have given 3 stars. However, this place was no more than "hip" restaurant that serves average asian food that's far worse than a lot of authentic places in chinatown and vietnamese establishments in washington ave, purely in the name of "fusion". I personally hate this type of place. By this type of place, here's what i mean: 1. menu is not coherent (they serve an array of things that are *asian* from thai, japanese, chinese, etc., without any real thoughts behind it...they are just...well, asian...) Why do I hate this thought? IMHO, it gives away the thought that asian is something you can categorize as Italian or French. Why not call a restaurant a European fusion and see what kind of menu we can come up with? 2. Asian BBQ Pork. Seriously? Don't just call BBQ pork Asian...each country (each region of each country) has very distinct taste... So you call something "asian bbq" because it resembles something in a regional Chinese cuisine? Come on... Just say what it is...five-spice, Korean chili paste infused, etc. It just seems ignorant. 3. The sashimi, dumplings, and whole fried fish...they were all average if not below average, compared to thai restaurants that serve whole fried fish, experienced sushi chef, or places in chinatown that serve dumplings. So putting them all in the same place justifies the food being average because the place has a bit of everthing...i don't think so. 4. The place is just too "hip". It probably has to make up in the ambiance for what it lacks in the food department. 5. Their "famous" lobster dish is no more than lobster with mashed potato, Morimoto's curry-spice infused lobster dish is a fusion I can be comfortable with; otherwise, just eat at the ethnic places. The only saving grace for this place, IMHO, is the dessert. Everyone in my party enjoyed the deserts: the dessert "bento", the tart, and the chocolate cake...they were all pretty good (the reason why they are getting 2 stars).
label: NEG

text: The first time I used Absolute Carpet Care I had no problems. The guy came out and cleaned my vacant two bedrooms, living room, dining room and long hallway for $100! I even referred multiple friends to their service! I booked my most recent appointment with Dot. My new place is about half of the size of my last place. In addition, I moved all of my living and dining room furniture out on my patio. My bedroom furniture takes up majority of the carpet space, so I expected to pay no more than what I had paid before. I waited for the technician who showed up over 1 hour late with no explanation! He pulled a dirty, portable carpet cleaning machine out of the back of his pick up. Their machines are not even truck mounted! He walked around my front room and handed me an estimate of $300 for the living room, dining room and a small chaise lounge! The technician said it was so expensive because of the stains in the dining room. I insisted that I only wanted a basic carpet cleaning, coupon price $59.99. The dining room carpets obviously needed to be replaced but this is a rental and I just wanted to have them disinfected. (My family had a carpet cleaning company-I understand carpets) He refused to just clean the carpets without charging me for the spots. He started to clean the living room and I stopped him and asked if he was going to clean the bedrooms first so he didn't drag his dirty equipment over the clean carpets....He dropped his wand and said he didn't even know he was scheduled to clean the whole house and the bedrooms would cost an additional $100! Bringing the total to $400! I was of course upset and immediately called Dot (the person I set the appointment with) as well as Greg the owner. text: Everything here was ok, but only some things were great. I thought about three stars, but I'd have to say the appetizers alone were enough to bump my rating up to four. We had a tart and moules that were quite inspiring. Unfortunately my entree of frog legs fell a bit short of the expectations raised by the apps. The breading was so very delicious, but the meat itself didn't seem to have any seasoning and not much flavor. The slaw with it was also a near miss. Other entrees at our table included rabbit fricassee with an awesome fresh pasta. The rabbit was just a dash of seasoning shy of heavenly. The duck confit was pretty tasty, but again, just shy of what I would get excited about. Finally, the steak salad was really impressive. Like the tart and moules appetizers, it demonstrated that perfection can be found here. Hopefully the kitchen will continue to pursue the last few tweaks to make the entire menu a knock out. The service was great, there were several attractive options on the wine list and the place has a nice bistro feel. I will certainly continue to visit Meauxbar to see how things are going.

text: My California friends almost flipped their lids when they heard I had never tried In-N-Out Burger. I had heard of the fabled chain from the Big Lebowski, and almost everything from that movie is gold. These friends promised a heavenly experience as they swooned at the suggestion that In-N-Out Burger was soon to be available here in good old Tucson. Because I was totally inexperienced, and would have never really stopped there without a strong suggestion, they dragged me there and even bought my first meal there. We paraded outside for a quick lunch, which is definitely cool for a fast food joint--outside seating, who knew. I gobbled up the burger and fries, debating the subtleties of the flavors, textures, all the while taking in the decorum of the restaurant itself, the feel and atmosphere.... After I cleaned up my area, they turned to me and asked how it was. My only comment was, "Ever heard or had Steak'n'Shake?" They looked at me blankly...."You know, fun commercials, steakburgers, and shakes--'not a workaurant'?" The blank stares continued. Well, it is a good fast-food burger. It was certainly better than McDonalds or Burger King or Wendy's. But I've had better, and still prefer the late night rendezvous with Steak'n'Shake from my Midwestern days. Was it good? Yes, it's ok. Was it as good as everyone thinks? No, definitely not, and I highly recommend Steak'n'Shake for anyone that's never had it.

text: I stopped in for a quick bite. It was a random experience, to say the least, and I did not really have any expectations before going in. There was a pretty good selection of pizza. text: All of the yelpers are pretty spot on with this joint. When the boy suggested that we do an Italian BYOB on our trip up to Philly to see the NIN concert I, of course, turned to Philly Yelp for insight. Lo and behold, La Viola turned up as a solid Italian BYOB and was open until 2300 hours on a Friday night. It was on. Cozy, cramped quarters where you're pretty much sitting elbow-to-elbow with other (often Italian-speaking) diners next to you. Fortunately, we arrived circa 2230 and the place had pretty much cleared out, so we had a giant table toward the back (or as back as it gets in their little dining space) all to ourselves. The wines that I'd pulled out of my stash of Linden Vineyards stuff worked out incredibly well, and I think the wine made the meal more than anything else. The bread that everyone else raved about was totally charred for us. Unimpressive - I had a piece before giving up. The Vitello Alla Viola I ordered had a great rich sauce with savory 'shrooms and crunchy prosciutto sliced more like pancetta than the thinly shaved prosciutto I'm used to. The veal itself was surpassingly tender, but didn't seem to have any flavor on its own. Moderately priced at $15 - I certainly wouldn't consider it a steal, but completely acceptable. I think the star of the evening was the ricotta cheesecake paired against our Linden Vidal Riesling. Our waters were tended to, but my g/f's pita bread was late five minutes on one occasion until the waitress looked over and remembered. Mona's seems to me to be a generally themed middle-eastern restaurant, though I have no clue as to what part of the mid-east that is and I don't think they do either. The first time I came here I got the gyro platter ($10), and the second time I got a single gyro ($4). The gyro platter is appetizing enough; meat is hot and cooked well, hummus, fresh lettuce, and a bit of tahini sauce. It sort of works like a fajita gyro. The meat was good, lettuce was fresh, hummus was fine if not somewhat out of place, but the tahini sauce, although interesting, failed to take the place of tzatziki. Tzatziki is like the perfect counterpoint to the savoriness of gyro meat, and tahini just seems like a poor bitter substitute to me. And I didn't even get any tahini sauce with my single gyro order on my second visit. Of course, I don't know if this is normal in mid-eastern cooking, but to me, it just wasn't as good. Of the other items on the menu some proved worthy and others just odd. I've never really liked grape leaves, but I tried some of my g/f's and they were quite delicious. Their hummus is pretty good. I ordered fried kibby ($4.59) as an appetizer. It's some sort of wheat/ground beef crust stuffed with ground lamb and pinenuts. Sounded good, but I tasted more salt and bland meat than anything else. If I go back, I'll probably try the meat grape leaves, or just order the vegetarian ones. Their lamb chops look good but expensive ($15). Their prices on most of their menu are good, which is somewhat redeeming. I wish this was my gyro-spot, but it's not. 1 star for unimpressive but filling, cheap food. 1 star for decent service and having a deli with pretty fresh pita bread and an assortment of middle-eastern kietsch.

text: How adorable is place? Very. I spent a lovely weekday morning here, and was so awed by all the displays and activities available. But you know, as someone who's been studying Early Childhood Education, it was only fitting that I go, right? Why, sure. First floor: - Oh, come on. You know you want to touch that plasma ball. - That rock wall? It's really for kids. I'm a little over 5 feet, and I could reach the top in two steps. - You must see that screen with all the colors that captures your movements and poses. That is just soooo awesome. Don't be shy - dance in front of it. Jump around. You'll love it! - Team Turtle Training Camp. That's where I sang a song about not smoking, created a well-balanced meal, and learned how to express my feelings. Yup. - There's a mat where you can practice your *STOP, DROP, & ROLL* skills. In the same area, you can learn how to make emergency phone calls. (Uh, no, I didn't do that.) - I found out I can throw a baseball at 30something mph, and reaffirmed that I can't throw a football to save my life. - The theater is nice and cozy, but I had just missed the show. I did get to take a picture with Stuffie, though. (And I'm still sad I accidentally deleted it.) - THE PULLEYS. Those were so much fun, as was the lever and this other corner where you can capture your shadow. (Tip: close your eyes as the flash is about to go off, because that is freakishly bright.) SECOND FLOOR: - The bathroom is something spectacular. - There's a play area for the very little kids. I'm sure if I were two years old, I would have loved it. - I'm quite impressed by the exhibit dedicated to the eye. It's like all the information on the eye that I learned in elementary school was crammed into this place. - As sticky as it was, I did like to play with bubbles. I didn't get to stand in this one place where you can try to enclose yourself in a giant bubble, though. - The roleplay areas were so cool! I wish I had a big cabin, a canoe, a crane, a ship, and a cafe to play with ... even now. And that grocery store where you can actually "go shopping" and stand in a "Three items or less" line? How precious is that? - I loved the Mr. Rogers' Neighborhood exhibit. Wow, what a fit of nostalgia that gave me. I could play in the Neighborhood of Make-Believe. I could even open a closet and put on a sweater. You know, if I wanted to. There's something so fun about acting like a kid, and this was a place where I could do just that. For a "grown-up," this place would probably be boring. It may seem small, but it's probably the size of a country to some child. Say what you want, but it was like a big playground for me. I love how something so simple can bring you back to that attitude of a child, where everything is so interesting and so new. I thought this place was great for both adults (with some use of the imagination, of course) and children, and so worth the $7 admission. If I ever find myself in New Orleans, I'd definitely visit again. (PS - the website says you can rent the museum?! And we're not talking about for your nephew's sixth birthday party - but a reeeal event. HOW AWESOME. Okay, now I wish I lived nearby so I could take advantage of that.)

text: (This is for the Hillsborough location.) I'm from California which features an embarassment of good, cheap Vietnamese restaurants. Chauvinistically, I wasn't expecting much from this place, but I went anyway, desperate for some of that delicate Vietnamese flavor I love so well. I shouldn't have worried. The food was very good. We began with the Chao Tom Nuong, which is the do-it-yourself spring roll with ground shrimp pattie ($11.95). The price may be somewhat high but the platter was absolutely tremendous, and they boil the rice-paper wrappers for you instead of leaving it up to you, unlike other places.The plate came with the shrimp, pickled radish and carrot, mint leaves, cucumber, and a big pile of vermicilli noodles with friedd garlic on top - delicious.The shrimp pattie was delicious with a taste somewhat indicative of dim-sum, and the vegetables accompanying were very fresh. However, they didn't give us any cilantro! We moved on to our lunch choices. I ordered the Bun Muc Nuong ($7.50) which is Grilled Squid over vermicelli noodles, although I added a portion of grilled shrimp for a few bucks extra. The seafood was tasty and had a good charred taste, although the squid got just a little bit too soft. The bowl provided a generous portion of vegetables along with the noodles - in fact, it was definitely the biggest vermicelli noodle bowl I'd ever seen. (Portions are always bigger in the South...even in Vietnamese restaurants.) I poured a big bowl of fish sauce over it and went to town. Delicious, fresh, and marginally healthy. My grandmother had the Bun Cari Ga or Curry Chicken Soup ($6.50) which came in a tremendous bowl, along with fresh vegetables (cilantro, mint, bean sprouts, jalepeno) for garnish. It had a rich coconut milk flavor and was full of chicken, carrot, eggplant, and potato, along with the standard rice noodles. It was very tasty, but so gigantic that she could barely finish a third of it. (I sense a VERY cheap way to eat for at least two days.) The restaurant is set in what was an old steakhouse space and it looks it - very big and not too bright inside. Seating is at booths, and wooden chopsticks are provided to you without asking. Our server was quick and efficient - food came out at a steady clip, despite the restaurant seeming to do a booming business at lunch time. Conclusion: Very good Vietnamese food in a somewhat unlikely part of town. I'll definitely be back next time I find myself in Tampa.

text: Ooh, Satellite Café. I love the kind of café i can sit in for HOURS and be perfectly content just admiring the things they've got hanging (or painted) on the walls and ceilings and being delighted by the people I see walk through the door and sit for a spell. The ambience of the place garners five stars.-- very warm, welcoming, and spacious enough to make every visit a new experience depending on where you sit and what perspective of the place you take. Super props for the hand-mosaicked tables, pochoir stencils on the walls, eccentrically skillful menu board illustrations (I can't wait to see what'll replace the witches stirring a cauldron for the winter...), ample supply of board games and books, varying types of seats (couches, chairs, high stools, regular old tables for two and four). The tea menu also is quite good. However, at least three teas that I've attempted to order have been "out". This leads me to wonder how often these teas are actually replaced... I really want to try a few that sound delicious, but they never seem to be stocked. Finally, ONE negative point: I once bought a day-old muffin that tasted like reconstituted dog food. Since it was day-old, there was no label, so it might have catered to a certain dietary persuasion, but it was plain old bad. I threw it in my trash can at home and later found that my cat (who eats eeeeverything) had dragged the thing out onto the floor, hungrily ripped it apart, and ultimately poo-pooed it (meaning: left it lying on the floor, not "poo-pooed" in the literal sense...). Actually, one more negative point: customer service does leave a little to be desired, depending on who's behind the counter. One night around 5pm I went in and ordered a Bike Shop Bagel, only to be sarcastically belittled as such (somewhat hyperbolically paraphrased): "PSSHHHH BAGEL? Are you SERIOUS?! We ALWAYS run out of bagels. DUH. No one in their right mind tries to order a bagel after 4pm !!! What a LOSER! Have you even BEEN here before ?!" Needless to say, I was not thrilled, especially seeing as I had often ordered a Bike Shop Bagel after 5pm in the past, but I did consequentially realize that the Bike Shop Wrap (which I ended up ordering, when I should have just thrown my hot tea in the barista's face and stormed out) is also really good and gives you almost twice the innards as the bagel for only a buck more. Despite sometimes crappy customer service, the space itself --and its menu selections-- is wonderful, so I give the place five stars with the suggestion to make Satellite part of your repertoire... because maybe then the counter people won't be so sour/apathetic to you in the future :) !! SECRET TIP: Bike Shop Bagel on a Cinnamon Raisin is GO-O-OD! ! ! Try it !

text: Unforunately, I can't give a place 0 stars, but I can sum up my experience here in one word: BLECH! We ate here some months back and the experience was so bad that it still haunts me. Here's what I think of when I think of Mediterranean food: fresh, wholesome, light, healthy, sunny-flavored food. Athenian Gardens is none of these things. It's bland, heavy, and ham-handed, and I am being kind when I say that. I understand that restaurants need to cut costs, but it was painfully obvious how much cost-cutting they'd done here (at least I hope that's why the food sucked so badly, at least that's a respectable excuse). The grape leaves were soggy and oily, and I am not sure how they managed to remove the tang from a pickled leaf - it's some sort of diabolical miracle. The tabouleh was nothing but unseasoned, overcooked bulgur with just a few miserable and mealy flavorless tomato chunks and a sprinkling of DRY parsley and a generous drenching of cheap olive oil. The hummus was laughable and lemon-free. The falafels were limp, without even a hint of crunch, and tasted like wet little sawdust pucks. My boyfriend had a chicken pita wrap - the chicken was rubbery and obviously microwaved and arrived swimming in some sour cream nightmare that I believe was supposed to be tzatziki sauce. Either these people are completely clueless or the kitchen is performing a completely genius work of dry, black-as-night comedy at the patrons' expense. To add insult to injury, our server was sullen and absentee...well not absentee, just absent from the tables. She was so busy standing with her back to us and the other two tables staring out the window that after waiting 15 minutes for her to come by, we just decided to walk up to her to tell her we wanted to send our food back. She then tried to argue and tell us the food was good. I told her it was obvious that our meal had at least partially been microwaved and she then stopped arguing and told us there would be no charge. That was the high point of this experience. Hopefully their other locations are nothing like this, but after this meal I don't dare find out...I'll try every other Mediterranean spot in the bay area first. We arrived here STARVING and were hoping to catch a quick bite, but the food was so awful that we each tasted a single bite of everything and decided we'd rather pick some stuff up at Publix and make our own lunch. Thankfully the poor quality of the food ruined my appetite for a while, so at least I didn't leave Athenian Gardens hungry!
