text: December 2nd was the beginning of a hopefully prosperous collaboration between yelp and the Arizona Theater Company. This event prompted me to go to an event I may have otherwise passed by, which ultimately would have been unfortunate. I'm not typically a patron for theater, but do have a deeply seated appreciation for music and history. And the current performance, "Woody Guthrie's American Song" squarely strikes to the heart of these subjects. The performance centers around the music of America's original and arguably most genuine troubadour as well as the political and natural calamities that helped shape it. Set in the 1930's and 40's, times were certainly tough all over. The dust bowl and oil busts in the midwest led to mass migrations of folks to the West in search of jobs that ultimately were not there. The Great Depression struck to the soul of every American who lived through it. Then the US was pulled into WWII. All the while, Woody Guthrie put pen to paper in a way that no other could (although he'd vehemently deny that!). He was able to do so because he lived through those events, as opposed to merely observing them. He hit the streets, he hit the rails, he hit the fields and camps. He watched and he listened to all that went on around him. He penned songs about everything he observed. Even through all the hardships these times had to offer, somehow these songs were able to resonate a... positivity, an uplifting spirituality, a message of hard times but solid hopes that almost seems contrary to everything going on. But it wasn't. It just took someone who could remind people that they "ain't gonna be treated this old way." And that someone was Woody Guthrie. With the state of affairs in this country today, it's somewhat tempting to draw corollaries to those tough times in the early-mid 1900's. Times certainly aren't as tough now (for most) as were then, but still, the present needs a good reminder of the songs--the lessons--of Woody Guthrie. And this presentation does just that. The acting is professional, the music top notch. The presentation might be a little confusing until you realize there are more than one character representing Woody. But ultimately, it works. More so, a performance such as this just fits perfectly in a stunning theater like Tucson's Temple of Music and Art. For someone like Guthrie, who fit such an epic life into such a short time--he died at only 55 years of age--you might think it would be hard to fit his biography into a 2 hour performance. And you'd be correct. If you've studied the life of Guthrie at all, you are not likely to learn anything new in this performance. But I don't think a biography is really the intent here. Instead, as stated earlier, this is really about Guthrie's music and the way it was shaped by the surroundings. And that comes across nicely. Historic photographs hauntingly cycle above the stage, giving a glimpse into the hard times faced, poignantly contributing to the raw emotions that the actors convey. A minimalist set serves to keep the spotlight on the emotion displayed by the absolutely competent suite of actors. In short, it's not necessarily a lesson in history, nor is it necessarily a biography of Woody Guthrie. Instead, it is a series of snapshots on America, only possible because of the foundation laid by a true American traveler--a true American--as long as 75 years ago. By the way, tickets may seem steep at the range of $36-$59, but for that price, you are getting a performance of caliber that is befitting to any professional theater production. In other words, treat yourself this holiday season, lay down the cash, and go see it for yourself.

Despite the unnecessarily loud techno music and the distinct feeling that I was underdressed, I enjoyed perusing the eclectic collection of sculptures and paintings by various artists from around the country. Walking around the balcony of the Arcade to the Show Room, I was surprised by how many people had come out for the Art Crawl, from hipsters to older couples to young families. Other attractions included some kind of audience participation painting experiment and a keyboard player performing eerie songs on the ground floor of the Arcade. The Crawl turned out to be an accessible, laid-back community event that serves to expose Nashvillians to a range of visual art.

text: i wish my favorite artist (joseph arthur) would find somewhere else to play. yes, the one thing this venue has going for it is some excellent sound - IF you stand in the right place. best place to witness this is from halfway back (i'm talking about the downstairs here) near the soundboard. any further back, and unfortunately you'll get more bar noise than guitar noise. other good points... the ticket guy at the counter is nice. and the positives end there for me. anyway, so if you're in the right spot, the sound is glorious. last week i saw joseph arthur thrice (one show at wcl, one in nyc at the bowery and once in hoboken at maxwell's). the wcl show trumped the others in terms of sound, but was the worst of the three shows. i blame the wcl. text: check another one off the list!! My friend again seared his tongue on the chicken pot pie right out of the oven (the beignets had come right out of the fryer! haha), but after a few minutes we both were able to appreciate the homey chicken and dumplings flavor. we agreed it was on the light side for a pot pie, more brothy and not overwhelmingly rich or creamy. he got a glass of Coppola's Director's Cut Zinfandel which was much richer than my glass but perfect for dessert. all of the desserts sounded good to me, so to go along with the rest of our meal i chose the most southern, Apple Pan Dowdy a la mode. YUM!! it was like a baby apple pie, complete with a small lattice crust that was crunchy and flaky. they know how to make all different kinds of great dough here! the apples were warm but not mushy, and the vanilla ice cream was in the perfect amount and high quality. i would love to come back as i enjoyed the food and the atmosphere, the bar area looks cool with a lot of outside light and black and white checked tile floor. i want to try the pork chop with ginger, thyme, sweet potatoes and spring veggies, the steak frites (smelled like wonderful steak grilling when we walked in!) and the chicken adelicia with fontina and tomato chutney aioli. and of course i want to try all the desserts. :) particularly the chocolate sheba, described by our waiter as a fudgy thing with dried fruit and nuts.

We were there to celebrate a birthday - someone who always gets slighted because her special day falls on Thanksgiving weekend. We told the waiter, just in passing we were celebrating. Needless to say, after acknowledging he heard us, he didn't say another word. Not even a "Happy Happy." We weren't looking for anything, seriously, except a little verbal cheer. As for the food, it was O.K., not great. Special rolls were average at best. The service was awful - waiter was a teacher who acted like he was doing us a favor taking our order. Save your money. Hit another sushi bar and then head to one of Nashville's great bars to people watch. Unless of course, you don't mind feeling like you're back in high school and you're not part of the cool crowd.

Decor was not as nice as I expected from Olde City. I usually don't dine in that area, but when I do, I expect some modern, posh decor. It looked empty, dark and a bit rundown. I usually love karaoke if its in the right atmosphere... but if its restaurant week and we are trying to have a nice chill date night out, you really should mention that somewhere on your website or on the phone that there will be live singing that night of varying talent... it would have been a dealbreaker. I received my express checkout bill under the door and realized they had charged someone else's credit card for my parking charges. Not a good thing. text: Protzel's is AMAZING. They have the best quality corned beef and turkey of any deli I have ever been to. People will always tell you that this place is like a Jewish deli you would find in New York. WHERE is this Jewish deli everyone so easily recalls from their New York travels?? I have lived in NYC for four years now and have yet to find this supposedly common New York experience. Maybe they once existed around the time Protzel's came to be, but today the supposed best delis in NYC are over priced tourist traps that have nothing on Protzel's in terms of quality and taste. To further my point, the best deli according to New York Mag is a "Montreal" style deli that is a better version of the smoked meat shops that you actually find in Montreal run by recent law grads who could not find a job in the wake of the recession and wanted to improve upon something from their undergrad memories at McGill. People lucky enough to live in St. Louis: Rejoice in the glory of Protzel's- It may very well may be the best Jewish deli in the world! (at least that's what any true new yorker would proclaim)

text: one would think that having lived in the yunk for 8 years i would have known about the brew pub's all you can eat brunch feast. but, sadly, no... well, not until today! tho quite pricey considering that i don't NEED to eat the amount of food necessary to warrant the steep $21 cost, i did do my best to get my money's worth (and haven't needed to eat anything else since!) my made-to-order veggie omelet prepared @ the omelet station was huge & delicious and would have been a meal aplenty for me...but alas, i loaded up additional plates with roasted potatoes, half a bagel with cream cheese & veggies, fresh fruit salad, french toast with blueberry sauce and an assortment of pastries. a ton of food, right? yet i didn't even scratch the surface!!! there was SO much more, including more lunch-y dishes like meatballs and chicken marsala that didn't stand a chance at getting on my meat-free plate. coffe/tea is included in the set price....not mimosas/blood marys...but they're a pretty decent deal at only $3.50 a glass. servers don't have to do much here during brunch other than bring drinks and clear plates, yet our table of 11 seemed to have our mere 2 water carafes perpetually empty with no server in sight with whom we could request a refill. the BEST part: the live jazz band playing while you eat! that alone helped to turn what is a complete douchebag bar by nite into one of philly's classiest bunch experiences outside of a center city hotel. so while brunch was great, and the back deck can't be beat, the combination of the "eh" beers, the "ugh" late nite scene and the "huh? where'd ya go?" service definitely costs the brew pub a few stars.

text: Sometimes you get to a place and think you've officially reached the middle of nowhere. That is Carson's, most definitely. But once you get inside, you get a very TROPICAL vibe and that's what I want to emphasize. A small outdoor bar greets you in the front, and whether you're indoors or outdoors there's plenty of space 'dockside'. This is the type of low-key place that you'd expect to find on a beach at Club Med, Punta Cana, or Cancun. Now mind you, that means it's a slight bit cheezy but they've jazzed up that look with white tablecloths, outdoor heatlamps to sit by the water, and a more formal looking indoor area. text: If you are expecting the ambiance and flamboyance of Dolce, go to Dolce. If you are expecting fantastic homemade pasta and sauces, come to Porcini. What this tiny restaurant lacks in pizazz it makes up for in delicious food. We had the quatro bruschetta, scallops, a pasta special and the ravioli. All were absolutely fantastic. Like, last meal on earth fantastic. The desserts were above average, (we had ricotta cheesecake and flan) but not what you go there for. The portions were just right--everyone cleaned their plates but didn't over eat. The service was also fantastic. We opened up the restaurant at 5:30, and left around 8. We were the only ones there at the beginning, but the restaurant was quite full for a Monday night by the time we staggered home. I will be back as soon as I can!

text: I called Quarter Smith looking for antique or estate engagement rings and spoke with Ken. Since I don't live in the NOLA area, I asked about Quarter Smith's hours. Ken stated that his store is open from 7:30-2:30, Tues-Friday, but not on Saturdays. Since I wouldn't be able to get over there on a weekday, I asked if it would be possible to make a Saturday appointment. Ken laughed a little, as if this was a strange request, and said maybe, but that if I had an idea of what styles I was interested in, he would be happy to email pictures of any appropriate rings he had. I stated that I did know what I was looking for and described some styles to him. He asked me to send him an email with that information, anything else I could think of, and pictures of rings I liked from online or other stores. Since he seemed sincere, I went to the trouble of sending the email and pictures. He acknowledged my email, said he had some items that would interest me, and then I never hear from him again. ?!? I was in NOLA recently (having emailed Ken about a week before) so I stopped by his store and saw that it looked unused and nearly empty! When I got home, I checked the Quarter Smith website, which still appears well updated. However, the website states that the store is open from 9-4pm, Monday through Friday and Saturday by appointment. So what is the real story here? Beware this place, they will go out of their way to waste your time and are not at all interested in working around your schedule to serve you as a customer and make a sale. It's been at least a month and I've never heard from Quarter Smith.
label: NEG

Otherwise a tour, especially one such as a "vampire" tour which relies on hearsay, becomes not only a bore but an embarassment. I can compare Haunted History's Vampire Tour with the New Orleans Ghost Tour vampire tour and HH's guide didn't capture in this demanding role. My daughter and I took the NOG tour in 2004 and were entertained and delighted by the individual who acted much like a vampire himself with his top hat, cape and long nails. It's a fine line when your guide wants you to believe his stories and acts the part himself. He was able to pull this off whereas the HH guide stumbled over the stories and his amateur theatrics. He wanted us to think he was an expert but he told the same stories as the previous guide. It was telling that he had to beg for a tip and no one antied up a cent. The problem with a vampire tour is that the stories could occur anywhere at any building - it's all heresay. So while walking you all over the bloody place (especially on hot humid NO nites) the guide has to keep the group involved with stories and statements between the locations of interest. Our HH guide simply walked and talked to a couple of specific ladies. Several tips - One, with the vampire tour, be prepared for a disappointment if you get a corny guide. Second, the tours take a 15 - 20 minute break at the mid 1 hour of the 2 hour tour at a local tavern. It's a slight of hand to get you to buy a couple of beers or sodas. While it's nice to sit in the AC for a few minutes, only 5 individuals in our group of about 20 fell for this sell. You're already spending 20 bucks for natty stories - keep your money to yourself. Third, only tip the guide if you really did enjoy the guide's style. The stories are the same between the tours. Finally, try to stick close to the guide for incidental stories between the stops. Otherwise, you really only get the scripted stories which total about 5 each hour or so of your tour. Vampire tours are really a roll of the dice.

text: Eastern Connection Movers agreed to move our furniture and possessions from our house in Willow Grove, PA to a new house in Hatboro, PA. All arrangements were made over the phone. When the movers arrived on November 19, their truck was unable to fit up my driveway. Also, because the house is on a busy street (Route 63) the police would not allow them to park in front of the house. They had to park around the corner and trek through my neighbor's yard. After the phone arrangements had been made, George left us with the impression that his truck would be more than adequate to move all our furnishings and that the packing time would be approximately 5 - 7 hours. Around hour 9, the movers informed us that the truck would not be able to fit everything and they would "try" to have another truck for us in the morning. It had begun raining and the movers tracked mud into our house. At 10 PM on a Thursday night, we had to scramble to arrange for a steam cleaner for the carpet since the buyers had a walkthrough scheduled for noon the next day. We also had to contact many of our friends to see if anyone would be able to help us finish the move Friday morning should the movers not be able to obtain a truck. The chief mover and driver, Mike, told us that the owner usually got in at 7:30 and he would contact me with a solution. It took four phone calls from me starting at 7:40 before I heard anything. At 8:15 George called me to offer a cargo van. The van would not have fit the remaining furniture and we could not begin unloading in the new house until after settlement at 3 PM. Plus, they could not have gotten to my house from Upper Darby for at least an hour. I had to rent a U-Haul truck and arrange for a friend who was not working Friday morning to help me finish the move before the buyers walkthrough at noon. My wife and I feel that Eastern Connection Movers misled us. Their vehicle was not up to the task. They had to hire an additional mover once they started the job. They did not show me a contract until after they had loaded the truck. We felt coerced to sign the contract since they had the majority of our belongings on their truck. The time urgency ensured that we could not hire another mover. Eastern Connection Movers could have sent a representative to the house to determine whether it was a job they could handle. George's cavalier assurances over the phone indicate to me that he planned to take our money whether his one truck and three man crew could do the job or not. text: Two five star experiences, two three star experiences, one four star experience. Avoid restaurant week if you're just going out for a quick bite, and avoid the cantina hours unless your preferred dishes are on the cantina menu. I visited Distrito five times while I was in Philly. Two awesome experiences, and two mediocre experiences. I'm still going with four stars because no matter what, the food is delicious. My first experience was with a friend of mine who is a vegetarian. I happen to love most meat products whether by air, sea or land (mmm bacon), so we were both pleased at the menu selection having adequate vegetarian dishes that were quite tasty. In fact, one of them (huarache los hongos) was a repeat order for me on almost every visit (the 'almost' is a reason for one of the mediocre experiences). Service was fantastic, food was incredible, overall experience was a five star. My second visit was much along the same lines, but add the fact that we were able to sit in the Beatle and crack stupid taxi jokes all night, another five star experience. My two mediocre visits really had to do with special menus (one cantina, one restaurant week). On both occasions I had friends in town and wanted to show them Distrito and the incredible huarache los hongos. During restaurant week, we were limited to a very limited and high-priced menu. When you're going out for a cocktail and a quick bite, it was very limiting and really killed the experience for my friend. Garces has enough fans, but I wanted to get him one more. The really poor experience was when I took my girlfriend (who does not live in Philly) to show her one of my favorite restaurants in Philly. We went during the end of cantina hours. The cantina menu at that time did not have los hongos, so I asked the server when they would start serving the dinner menu. We were about 45 minutes away, so I asked if there was any chance we could get the huarache los hongos, and was told 'no'. No attempt to ask the kitchen, check with a manager, nothing. Just 'no'. I've worked in a restaurant before, and can understand if you're asking for paella during morning bakery hours, but this was nothing too extravagant and I'm sure the ingredients were already prepped for dinner. Needless to say, I was pretty displeased. When my girlfriend came back into town, we did not return to Distrito. My last visit was for brunch, where we had delicious food and decent bloody mary's (a little too acidic, although my stomach was not in great shape that morning...). All in all, this is a must-visit in Philly with amazing food. My recommendation is to check ahead on the menu that they're serving, and don't expect anything too much 'above and beyond' as far as service. Go for the great food and creative decor.

text: I was really excited about this bakery when I first read about it. I travel to France a couple times a year to visit family, and have a great appreciation for a good French bakery (which is practically every bakery in France). First off, I should note that their baguette is really good. One of the best in town. It's obvious that they use a good quality flour, as the flavor has just a hint of nuttiness. They are crispy on the outside, light and airy on the inside. That said, I was really disappointed by their food and pastries. Tartines (by definition) are served on baguette. Their tartines are served on a slice of (what appeared to be) sourdough bread. I got the shrimp guacamole tartine, and it contained six small shrimp with a very thin layer of avocado on a single piece of bread. Oh, it was served with a teeny tiny bowl of soup. All mine for $10. My partner got a slice of quiche, which was overcooked and served at room temperature (normally it should be served warm). Served with a salad of greens. Again, $10. In France a piece of quiche at a bakery costs two or three euros, it's twice the size of what we were served here, served warm, and tastes way better. We finished off with a Pain au Chocolat for dessert. It was nice and crispy on the outside, the chocolate was good quality (and not too sweet), and the inside of the croissant was absolutely dry and awful. No flaky layers. The pastry seemed really over-processed - it was not fresh enough, perhaps the butter was not good quality, and however the pastry was processed, it was not done properly. The thing looked great, tasted terrible. There are a few bakeries in town owned by French expats. It's a shame that they come here to open these businesses and call them "French Bakeries". With the exception of the baguette, I can do better at home. In France, these bakeries would quickly go out of business with those prices and that level of quality.

That was not out of haute wine tasting etiquette, but rather a clear preference to avoid drinking bad wine. The tasting room itself was festooned with surf boards and the like. I really felt they were targeting a younger crowd by offering up inexpensive wine choices with catchy labels and a friendly atmosphere. Amazingly this was one of the wineries featured in the movie Sideways. Inexplicable. Avoid.
label: NEG

text: This should be three stars, but the extra one goes out to the staff at The Wedge, who were some of the friendliest, genuine bar employees I've met in a very long time. Drinks are South-City Cheap (yay!) and they exhibit a nice selection of beer and liquor. Guinness is on tap so that makes me happy, too. The atmosphere is nothing like the surrounding neighborhood; and I would describe it as "lazy punk rock"... It 's a good thing! I visited their second floor for a show and was stunned to see a very crisp, clean bar area, complete with a small stage, video projection system and this ginormous red Mad Hatter-like couch that I will steal if I can find a backpack large enough. It's small and smoky so that might be an issue. Downstairs is a little more open, with a few hi-def tv's and a Big Buck Hunter video game machine. Nice! Apparently they're connected to (or own) a BBQ pit that offers a brisket and sweet potato fries... The carnivore in me wants to check it out again. Look out for an update!

text: As a connoisseur of junk-centric vegetarian food, I was happy to stumble upon Chilango's, a reasonably priced Mexican Food restaurant on State Street. It was refreshing to see a menu that incorporated vegan and vegetarian options that were not limited to your ubiquitous 'grilled veggie burrito.' The lady who took our order was down to earth and eager to help us out. I ordered the holy grail of all vegetarian burritos- a tofu burrito slathered in a sweet and savory mole. The burrito was a monstrosity, bursting at the seams with grilled cubes of tofu, black beans, rice, and veggies. The mole was delicious- and homemade (!!!!!). I was expecting to receive a burrito dosed with a jar of mole straight off the shelf of the ethnic food section in the grocery store- but this was totally not the case. The mole has a hint of honey and sweetness that I have never experienced before. For under twenty five dollars, my husband and myself (who are voracious eaters) were able to box up the leftovers and have a full meal for later. Chilangos is definitely worth checking out.

text: I really, REALLY wanted to recommend these people, because Silvia herself is very nice, and I have always been sweet and polite in my dealings with her. But after they DESTROYED my record of my children's heights written on the wall, I could not, in good conscience, keep working with them. It was like pouring acid over a cherished photo album, and I will confess I was and am still heartbroken. A year ago, they cleaned the knobs on my toaster oven, and in the process, scrubbed all the numbers off! It is hard to use a toaster oven with all the degree markings obliterated. They also cleaned a garage sink and completely flooded my garage with 30 gallons of water when they failed to replace a washing machine drain. To this, I would add that they do not clean ON TOP of anything above about 4 feet high, and routinely miss dirty fingerprints around light switches, etc. Remarkably, I had these folks clean my modest, 1,100 square foot tract home for TWO YEARS! Trust me - it's NOTHING fancy - more Jeff Foxworthy than Beverly Hills. So this was NOT a one-time aberration. I had to remind the cleaners to clean stuff like light switches, dirty windows, dirty venetian blinds, etc. EVERY SINGLE TIME - probably THIRTY TIMES, the same set of reminders. In fairness, they **ALWAYS** made the bathrooms shine. But they have zero clue about how to clean houses. I think most of their business is offices, not houses, and they are apparently a one-trick pony who cannot adapt to the unique requirements of homes. I detect from our conversations that Silvia has a "poor little me" mentality. For the record, Silvia owns a fleet of cars, has about 30 employees, a full office staff, and a huge commercial contract portfolio. She has far more employees than I do. When I have [on more than a dozen occasions] told her that her staff did not, for example, clean on top of the TV, which is about 5 1/2 feet off the ground, she explained that her cleaners were not very tall! Come on! I'm "only" 5'10" tall, and I when I clean my house myself, I have to stand on something to clean the top of the door jambs, which are nearly 7 feet tall. When I knock down cobwebs, I use something with a long handle. She needs to get a clue. Her explanation for grinding the numbers off my toaster oven dials was that her cleaners did not know anything about toaster ovens. WHAT?? This is a friggin TOASTER OVEN, not a nuclear reactor. Her cleaners may not be English literate, but they thought it was OK to scour until "ON/OFF" was gone??? ...till "100", "200", and "300" were gone from the temperature dial?? Last time I checked, Mexcio still used the decimal system and Arabic numerals!!! For the record, my hugely capable college intern spoke fluent Spanish and English, so language was not a problem. I speak a modicum of Spanish myself. When I hired Silvia's the first time, I gave them a full checklist to work with in resoundingly good Spanish - which they routinely ignored. I suspect Silvia hires people who represent themselves as good cleaners and does not spend a cent on training them, on standards, or on mid-level supervision or accountability. Her services are not cheap, and I suspect she has a good expense ratio, so I cannot believe she cannot afford training. She has zero concept of checklists, quality control, management, or organization, except for a grueling, metronome-like schedule. I assume most of her employees are recent immigrants, and no one has more appreciation for the difficulties faced by recent immigrants into a foreign culture than I do. However, Silvia bears the responsibility for educating her people in what the job requires. If your employees do not know what a stove is, that is YOUR problem as the employer, not theirs, and certainly not mine. I should be able to EXPECT your employees to know what a stove is. As an employer with nearly 3 dozen in your workforce, you should provide that kind of training. Don't know how to provide training? There are, like, a zillion companies who do it, and for competitive prices. You don't do your own tax, I'll bet. See - you already know how to hire outsourced services! For the record, Service Master, Coverall, and a zillion other cleaning services who hire recent immigrants DO train their workforce! I have had these people do a poor job for years, and all they flooded my garage, destroyed my toaster over, and destroyed my cherished records of my children's height as they grew up. I work 12 hour days, but will probably clean my home myself before I ever let someone in to do it for me again.
label: NEG

text: At the risk of sounding like a total bitch I have to post this...and it pains me. Until this happened- this place was actually our favorite sushi place. We used to come here at least twice a week. My favorite was the M.G. Roll (no avocado of course), the hamachi was always fresh and yummy. The chefs knew us by name and began preparing our 'usual' the second we walked in. I had been telling everyone how great it was, and had decided to bring my Mother and sister for lunch. We sat at a table towards the back, and everything was going great until they brought our crab rangoon appetizer. We LOVE crab rangoon. I ate mine quickly, so did my Mom. My sister, however, ate hers in slower bites. Upon biting into her first piece she looked at the inside to see what they had put into the rangoon. She leans over and asks me WHAT this black chunk thing was. It was about the size of my pinkie fingernail. After carefully examining the thing, we realized it was a bug. A big bug! We all started gagging at the realization of what that meant. In order for that bug to be inside a rangoon, it would have had to fall or climb into the mix, get scooped up and placed there and then deep fried. YUCK! Now, I realize that even the cleanest kitchens can have something happen- I've never seen their kitchen so I can't comment further. But in my opinion if this happens in your establishment- then you should probably comp the customers meal. But nope, not here. We pointed it out to the owner- he saw the bug for himself and offerred no recourse other than he wouldn't charge us for the appetizer (we were a la carte)This was extremely disapointing to me, as he knew that I was a 'regular'. Needless to say, we were not happy! Since we had already eaten a roll each by the time they had brought the rangoon- he felt that we should pay the bill, minus the rangoon. Apparently bugs in our food did not entitle us to a free roll of sushi. Sushi, that we would NOT have eaten had we seen the bug first. Another side note: Be wary of the sauce they put on everything. At first it tasted like Unagi Sauce, which we loved. But it had progressively began getting worse and saturating everything in it, is just icky. It became more bitter and had a cloying aspect to it. I heard some people remarking how good the sauce was, but it was not what it had been before. So if the chefs are reading this- whatever change you made to the sauce- is another reason why we don't come in anymore. It's possible that we'd have still given them another chance had they handled the bug incident better. This was our favorite place and we sang their praises and helped increase their business. It appears that we did that to our own detriment, because the quality and service went down in as they got busier. Bummer.
label: NEG

text: I had lunch here today, and I suddenly realized what gross neglect it has been to not write a review. The burgers - awesome. Get any toppings you want - the Bob special is pickles and jalapenos with ketchup. For a regular burger, they put two slabs on your bun, and its quite a mouthful. The fries - cooked in peanut oil, and as good as any Thrashers at the beach. And they give you LOTS. While you wait for your order, you get to fill your drink and wash it down with peanuts that you shell yourself. What could be better than that? The prices have risen over the years, and that's about the only reason I can't do five stars. This is a treat place for me, about every 2-3 weeks. Don't worry, you can work it off in that time.

text: Don't worry about the long lines; Pappy's is worth it. However, it is an imperative that you come early if you want 1) a short line; and 2) the full menu, as they do run out of certain options. The dry rub on the ribs is amazing; the sauces, while good, are completely unnecessary for the food being offered. Seriously, they maintain a smoker immediately outside of the restaurant. The pulled pork gets a bad rap from some on Yelp; however, it held up to strict scrutiny. The sides...ah, the sides...the sweet potato fries were amazing. They had the perfect balance of salt and sugar. The deep-fried corn had a slightly burnt tinge, but in general, the flavor was unique and a great match with the smoky BBQ flavor. A friend had the cole slaw and raved about it.

text: Santa Barbara Shellfish Company is located towards the end of the pier. It's a small restaurant with about 20 bar seating (indoors) and 16 outdoor seating (4 tables of 4). The wait during the dinner hour can be as long as 2 hours - but well worth it! Just don't forget to sign in on the clipboard when you get there. If the weather is nice, you can also skip the wait and order at the to-go station on the side of the restaurant. You can grab food there and enjoy it at one of the picnic tables by the pier. We ordered the steamed mussels, rock crab special, steamed lobster and oyster shooters. The seafood was fresh and simply prepared. Both the crab and lobster special were served with a side of soup (clam chowder or lobster bisque) and a small side salad. The sun went down while we were enjoying dinner and it became much harder to maneuver shellfish in the dark. The outdoor heater was also broken so it can get quite chilly. In all, it was a great Santa Barbara pier experience and we had a great time.
label: POS

text: I have been to Square One Brewery exactly three times. The first time, I was disappointed. The second time, I thought, "maybe I was wrong about this place." The last time simply made me remember never to second guess myself. Square One is a joke. Each time I've had shitty service (technically, I don't remember the second time due to drunken festivities, but I'm told it was terrible). One of my biggest pet peeves is servers that are rude--the amount of money that you make, to pay your bills, your food, etc, has a direct correlation to how nice you are. This last time, our server came over a total of three times--once for food/drink order, once for refill, once for check. We wanted to drink more, but the waitress wouldn't come over so we finally decided to go somewhere else. When I asked what she recommended for beer, she said "all of them." When I asked what she recommended for dinner, she said "it's all good." Then, at the end of our meal, she said that she couldn't split the ticket because of the size of our party--sure, that's understandable, except for the fact that the fucking table behind me that has more people, got theirs split up. Oh, and what's this? You already tacked on gratuity? No wonder you didn't come by, your tip was already taken care of; too bad bitch, I normally tip over the grat. Oh, the food. She finally told me that the pot roast was good. It wasn't. It was dry, and so was my friend's braised lamb. How the hell do you dry out meat that is prepared using a wet cooking method? Another friend had the fish and chips which I will grant is huge, but at least 40% of it was breading. The appetizers were also unimpressive, with the biggest failure being the calamari. I think I trust the seafood at LJS more than here. Anyway, the only reason that this place gets two stars is because it's ridiculously cheap. I guess that counts for something. But fuck you waitress; you're the Shark to my Jet.

text: The most basic lessons all philly food trucks have learned are somehow lost on the employees of Johnnie's. Way too expensive, poor service and low quality. I ordered a hot sausage and diet pepsi, which came to over $7; my mistake was thinking that this would translate into something special. Amazingly it takes 5-10 minutes for them to produce any order, despite the fact they have 2-3 people working there. My order sat behind the bald cashier until I pointed it out. I completely understand why people are upset. Yes, it's "just" hot dogs, but does the place have to be so bad? My only guess as for why Johnnie's is still in business is that Main Line'ers are somehow duped into equating quality with price, or some form of cognitive dissonance, where it's too painful for them to admit they've been cheated. I'll close with a message of hope: I would like nothing more than to have a solidly good dog on the Main Line; judging from other people's reviews, this is currently an under-served market, and perhaps a great opportunity for an aspiring entrepreneur.

text: This is now named Home-style Beijing even though the receipt still says Green Leaf. I went there today with my wife and teenage daughter. Though not specified anywhere the lunch specials were not offered on a Saturday. That was no big deal. 12:30 on a 72F. sunny weekend, it was deserted when we arrived. We ordered the scallion pancake as a sharing app (reminiscent of the Thousand Layer Bread at Rangoon) and also the pot stickers (but asked for them steamed, instead of fried.) We were probably being a little too health-conscious. The dumplings were water-logged, and so masked the flavor of the gingery ground pork. Also the squirt of hot water in your mouth when you bight into a dumpling is not particularly pleasant. My daughter is the least adventuresome of the trio, and ordered pan-fried thin noodles with chicken. It was an somewhat interesting dish, with a curiously seasoned brown gravy over the usual bamboo shoots, mushrooms,carrots and onion. Perhaps a hint of five-spice powder. I ordered the Mao's Pork belly with a little trepidation, as pork belly can sometimes be pretty fatty. It was not, but as advertised, it was pork in a sweet sauce with peppers (bell and dried hot.) Not a bad dish, and enough to share. You would definitely want to order dome kind of veggie dish along with it though. What killed the meal for us was my wife's dish, double-cooked pork. When it arrived, we were wondering if the waiter had brought the wrong dish. Was that tofu ?? Maybe eggplant ?? The shiny, flabby squares certainly did not look like any kind of pork we had experienced prior. Upon close inspection, there were tiny ribbons of meat along the edges of SOME of the squares. Sure enough, they were pork. The lion's share of the slices were PURE FAT. Though it took a long time to get the waiter's attention (as it did later to get our check, despite the fact only one couple arrived during our meal) when we asked if this was normal, he assured us that this was the way they make it. Now I realize this is touted as authentic Beijing cuisine, and maybe it is. But when you also have Wonton Soup and Sweet and Sour Chicken on your menu, I think it might be nice to apprise an obvious Western family if a standard dish like "Twice Cooked Pork" varies THAT widely when prepared to authentic Beijing standards. The waiter asked if he should take it off the bill. We though they should take it off the freakin' MENU, but said yes, only because it was inedible. It was like lightly sauteed fatback. Maybe it was a purely unlucky choice, but IMO, unless you are specifically known for REALLY off-the-wall authenticity, it should be the waiter's duty to inform an unsuspecting diner if a dish may potentially be unappealing to even above-average tastes.

text: I just can't give 5 stars, unfortunately. My recent visit on Oct. 21st was great overall but not the world-class experience that this restaurant used to be under the original ownership. While it is still the best steakhouse I've been to, it can't compete with it's own memory. This is not the same Bern's as it was in the 1980's when I took my Prom date their for dinner. Back then I'll admit to being a little 'out of my league' and awestruck as an 18-year old with an affinity for steak and no experience with wine at all. The experience made a huge impact on me. I can remember the finest French Onion soup, the best Bleu Cheese dressing I'd ever tasted and, of course, a Filet Mignon that melted across my teeth...pure dining bliss! I spent the next 27 years learning to cook myself and honing my palate for wines and learning different vineyards and varietals to pair with different meals. It was a lifelong goal to one day return to Bern's with the knowledge and experience to re-create that memory but as a much more sophisticated diner worthy of their expertise. Back then we showed up in rented tuxedo's and a borrowed car; this time we showed up in my Cadillac wearing my tuxedo and since I had been in email and phone conversation with their Sommeliers for a week prior to the meal, I was assured all would be in-place for me to show my wife, my sister and her new husband a dining experience of a lifetime. The Sommeliers messed up my sparkling wine vintage request and were totally out of the Merlot I had been in contact with them for a week prior to my reservation asking about. In addition, the server seemed completely unaware that I had been in contact with Eric and the others about the wines I was interested in. The Sommelier on staff tried to compensate with another vintage of comparable quality but that's not the point. The whole reason for having Sommeliers and giving the diners access to them is to ensure you can prepare your dining experience in advance and know what you are getting. What's the point if they are not going to have the wine they say they have when you get there, even after asking for it? What's the point of asking specifically for the 2000 Domaine Le Reve and end up getting the 1998 vintage? Rooky, amateurish mistakes by the supposed "best of the best." A very disappointing experience from that perspective. Now, I will say that I am now a fan of the new cut, the Chateaubriand, and both my sister and I had very well cut and properly cooked steaks of that type. I could not tell if my new Brother-in-Law's steak was prepared correctly but he enjoyed it enough and had no complaints. My wife's Filet Mignon, however, was over done. She asked for Medium-Rare and they advertise a "true Medium-Rare"...she got Medium, plain as day. The Bleu Cheese dressing had such small chunks of bleu cheese in it that it was hardly 'impressive' and my wife claims to have had a better French Onion soup elsewhere. The fact that they have also lowered the dress code was also a bit upsetting. That's what they have Side Bern's for right? Dressed in tuxes and evening gowns and surrounded by people in jeans and Polo shirts was a huge downgrade to the atmosphere. I know it's a tough economy but that's a bit like sitting next to someone in shorts and flip-flops at a Broadway show. The desert room saved the evening overall, as the server was delightful and the Bananas Fosters and 6-Rum Alexander's helped to numb the disappointment. I did not complain at the time, as I didn't want to ruin the experience for my guests, who may not appreciate the subtle differences in different wine vintages or a slightly over-cooked steak...but I do and I was disappointed in the changes from the original concept. Do you know they don't stock any wines over $10,000 a bottle anymore? In 1984 they had a vintage Rothschild's that went for over $23,500!

text: When I saw Tinto on the list of participating restaurants in the Dining Out for Life event, I was thrilled and made a reservation. My friend and I had talked about going for months, and this seemed like the perfect opportunity. The reservation was made two weeks in advance on Open Table, when there were still plenty of time slots available. When we arrived at the restaurant, we were seated at the four top closest to the front door. Looking around the small room, I figured it was better to be by the door and in a comfortable booth than seated at the banquette along the other wall, with very little space between tables. It wasn't until I got up to use the ladies' that I saw the many tables in the next room with the bar, plus all the cozy seating downstairs. I had table envy. One person in our party was running a bit late, so we started with a round of drinks. The red sangria was pretty awesome. When our group was eventually complete, the dining room was in full swing and our server was definitely not as available. A drink was spilled on our table and another server came to help clean up. Eventually, our guy came back to take our order. We had some picky eaters at our table (not recommended when dining with a group at a tapas restaurant, BTW), so between the four of us, we ordered a few lighter items to share and then each person picked one or two more substantial plates for themselves. In the meantime, another round of drinks was ordered, and the unusually long wait had some wondering if grapes were being stomped out back. A complimentary plate of cheese crisps started the meal. Everyone enjoyed these with the accompanying dipping sauce. Soon after, we received a double order of Serrano wrapped figs. They were good, but we all agreed that the coarse sea salt sprinkled on top was unnecessary. Several minutes later, we received a dish of olives. They were small and very garlicky, and at this point in the meal, I was ready for something more substantial. As plates were dropped one by one, nothing that I ordered was appearing. Now, I've eaten in tapas restaurants many times (including Garces' own Amada and Distrito), but the timing between each dish was so long that when our server asked how we were doing, my sangria got the best of me and I could only think to reply, "Hungry." Eek. Not very ladylike! Eventually, we received the rest of our plates, each one spread out over more time than was necessary. My friend's tuna tartare sandwich looked amazing, as did a crab dish that another member of our group enjoyed. Despite reading mixed reviews on the organic chicken, I ordered it anyway and found it to be just okay, nothing extraordinary. The highlight for me was most definitely the mussels, which came shelled and served in a tiny pot with the most delicious tasting sauce and a side of perfectly seasoned frites with a lemon aioli at the bottom of the cup. This dish single-handedly salvaged my opinion of Tinto, which was not a high one before this point in the meal. Someone in our group remarked that there is always one table that gets the short end of the stick on a busy night, and it was unanimously decided that we were that table. When our server asked about dessert and coffee, it was a no-brainer that we cut our losses and move on. I do plan to return, maybe with just one other person next time, to give Tinto another shot. Despite our not so great experience, it was still wonderful to see so many people out to support an important cause.
label: NEG

text: To be honest, I don't really understand self-described "burger lovers." The few burgers that are outstanding, are outstanding because they're totally different from a normal burger, ergo making me a "unorthodox burger lover." Wait, that doesn't sound right. Anyway, I find The Fatted Calf to be ridiculous. How quaint, you're housed in a German inspired craftsman-ish building in the middle of corporate Clayton! And you serve burgers, how proletarian! It reminds me of celebrities that go to In-N-Out on first dates, its ironic charm. "I have all this money and fame, but I'm going to take you somewhere cheap to show you how cool and grounded I am!" To be fair, the burgers are solid and cooked perfectly. To be truthful, its expensive as hell. Burger, fries, mushrooms and a drink cost $22. American. That is redonkulous. The serving size of fries and mushrooms is a joke, especially at that price, and it boggles my mind that this place costs more than Peter Luger--like 30% more. How can you, a "modest" burger cafeteria in St. Louis, Missouri, cost 30% more than the most famed steakhouse in the five boroughs? I understand that $22 isn't a lot of money, but it is if you just want a burger, and that's all it is--a burger. FC makes a good burger, but so do a lot of other places in St. Louis for a lot less money. Save yourself some time and skip it. Unless you're Elisha Cuthbert, and you want to show me how Hollywood hasn't changed you. No, its cool baby, I believe you.

text: This place used to be better - I've been going to Nature's Food Patch for several years, its right down the street from my work and incredibly convenient. Unfortunately I've seen the store slowly declining in its quality and with the competition that has opened across the bay (Wild Oats and soon the Publix Greenwise marketplace) I find my visits less and less frequent. While I try to support the smaller, longer standing institutions even when the competition is priced less, I'm just repeatedly dissapointed with the direction this place has headed. I'm a vegan so shopping at a natural food store is pretty much a requirement to a well-rounded cupboard. Their grocery section is very adequate and actually priced quite reasonably when compared to other small natural food stores or even the big chains. I have, however, run into a frequent problem of purchasing vegan 'dairy' items and find that they are spoiled. This has happened to me on several occasions when purchasing fake cheese products, many of which were not even close to their expiration date, which leads me to believe that they may be improperly storing some of the food items that require refrigeration. For this reason I only buy dry good from them now. As for the deli, they made several improvements over the past few months but the quality and convenience has actually declined. To start off with the good, they do now have a hot food section which is great for lunch. No more bringing back cold lunches or having to reheat your meals in the company microwave! Also, they've expanded their racks to provide prepackaged foods from the deli cases including their pasta salads, tofu, and even sandwiches and wraps. Unfortunately, when they expanded the cases they did away with the convenient name tags that said whether or not items were Omnivore, Vegetarian, or Vegan. So now you have to ask the assistant behind the counter and the majority of the time wait while they scan the ingredients and give a not-so-helpful reply of, 'I think its vegan?" And while the prepackaged food is convenient so you do not have to stand in line... its been my recent experiences that prepared food in the deli has been suffering from quality controls that has lead to poor taste or even foreign objects in my wraps. Lastly, as someone whose been eating at the deli for several years, it would be nice if they brought in some new dishes for variety. To their credit, whenever I've had problems they've been very polite and offered to either exchange the item or offered me store credit. They seem sincere about improving the conditions but I see little change from visit to visit. When I shop here its for convenience and only for dry goods. Otherwise, I make a trip once or twice a month to Wild Oats and pickup a stockpile of my vegan essentials.
label: NEG

text: We had Mother's Day brunch here, $85 per person. (On Mother's day, brunch is served all day, we had a reservation for dinnertime.) Three stars for the food , minus 1 star for the service. The good part: they had a lot of high-end dishes using a lot of expensive ingredients (lobster, caviar, etc.) So why such a low rating? After having the brunch buffet here, I became convinced that high-end food can't be served buffet style. There were dishes that I could tell would have been good had they been cooked to order and not sitting out. It's really disappointing to have overcooked pasta or a cold escargot tart. And remember, for $85 / person, you can have a tasting menu at many restaurants where food is cooked to order for you. Another thing we discovered was that there was too much to try and too much going on. We got lots of little tastings of everything , but never had time to savor it. Before our mouth could savor an item, we had switched to another. Having a prix-fixe meal of 5-6 courses is much better -- sure you don't get to try as much variety, but then you really get to savor the different flavors and textures that the chef is aiming for in a dish. You let a dish grow on you and understand the nuance of a dish. Instead this buffet brunch is like taking the top 40 pop songs and taking a sentence from each stanza and just playing them right after the other. It's a mad slapdash of really good things - but you don't really have time to savor and enjoy. Service: OK, this can't be too hard considering it's a buffet service. Yet our service was not good. My boyfried and I like to use our expensive dinner dates as a time to talk and catch up on life , but instead it was like "go! speedracer go!'" to the next buffet table with these waiters. And, on top of that, the cheese was all terribly bland. The ravioli was pretty good--when you had any squash in it, they were incredibly skimpy on the squash and it was mostly just eating lumps of pasta. The octopus was TERRIBLE. there was little octopus and it was completely drenched in this disgusting, indescript brown sauce. You couldn't even taste the octpus, and at times even see it under this thick sauce. The scallops were cooked perfectly (I find it hard to get scallops that weren't overcooked). text: Went here with a bunch of co-workers for lunch. What others have said describes the place pretty well. It's a small place, is borderline clean and has minimal street parking. My one co-worker and I both ordered roast beef hoagies. Let me just say that this was the worst hoagie I've had in a LONG time. The roast beef was pale brown and tough, in other words, it was probably old. The meat was also riddled with fat and I picked out so much fat and gristle that I could hardly believe it. The taste of the hoagie left a lot to be desired. I asked my co-worker what he thought of his roast beef hoagie since I've found that he is usually less picky than me when it comes to food. He agreed that it was a pretty bad hoagie. It's a shame too because if it had been good roast beef....tender, pink and fresh....it probably would have been a good hoagie. One thing I'm surprised no one has mentioned in any of the reviews is the prices. For a sandwich joint, this place is pretty pricey. Expect to pay $8-$10 for a hoagie/sandwich (that's a sandwich only too - no fries, chips or pickles) and it's not like they are enormous or packed with any more meat than you'd find in hoagies at any other local pizza shop and for $3-$4 less. Add a drink to your order and you're up to close to $15 for lunch. There's no excuse for serving roast beef like I got on a hoagie (that should be reserved for swimming in a pool of gravy on a hot sandwich or maybe to give to the dog) so I would only go here again if I was really desperate and......scratch that.....I'd rather just go to the McDonalds around the bend for a quarter pounder.

text: Maybe I'm spoiled from all of the great tapas places I've been to when living in Chicago, but I just don't get the tapas scene in Saint Louis. Most of the places are very expensive for what you get, including the new Sanctuaria. Almost every selection was over 8 bucks and the food was neither your traditional tapas, or a fun new take on traditional tapas. Chicken strips, a pulled pork sandwich and shredded beef on mashed potatoes were all on the menu. Of course, they weren't described that way, but really you can put lipstick on a pig..but does that turn it into an interesting tapas dish?...no. I also ordered the featured drink of the day because I read a review that the bartenders there know how to make a good cocktail. The drink was the Gentleman's Touch..and while it was very tasty, and seemingly made with unique ingredients, I felt like I purchased an $8 tiny glass of kool-aid. My portion didn't even fit in a small martini glass. In summary, Sanctuaria feels like just another Saint Louis gimmick that is preying upon a population that digs the advancement of the grove area and is gambling that their patrons will like anything with an ethnic flair and nice decoration, and who will pony up their credit cards blindly for it.

text: A few years ago upon my first solo plane experience, I was rather anxious and worried about coordinating everything all on my own, getting to the airport and juggling all of my belongings. I'm a Fly Away regular and always depend on them to take care of me, making an anxious flyer relaxed and at ease. They make it all very simple with the check-in, baggage handling and drop off at the airport. Upon returning, I've never had to wait more than a few minutes to be picked up, and best of all my car is ready and waiting for me when I get back to the Fly Away office. A few times they've had bottled water waiting for me, too. The staff are all very nice. The drivers are always very friendly and courteous. text: I know, I know, I say this all the time--when you rate/review something, you're making a comparison; I think "x" is amazing because I've had "y." With this in mind, once again, I'm left with a headache inducing conundrum. Do I rate the Deacon under the "dive bars with food" category, or do I rate them as a regular restaurant? I've been here a few times now, because I wanted to check on their consistency. Here's what I know: 1.) The hummus and sweet potato salsa are both excellent (and I have a firm dislike of sweet potatoes) 2.) Their salads, while not amazing, are definitely solid. Kudos to you Deac, for making your own dressings. 3.) The curly dog sandwich is definitely unique, and also delicious. The fish and chips are decent. The veggie boudin burger wasn't to my liking, but then again, I'm the guy that would order "pork" if they offered it as a side dish. However, I'm going to agree with Nowell in saying that it is refreshing to try a veggie burger that doesn't taste like every other veggie burger--the lady seemed to enjoy it. 4.) Their vegan pineapple upside down cake was toted as "so good, you won't know it's vegan." Yes, yes you can tell it's vegan. Fail. Fire your copywriter. 5.) Their jukebox is pretty amazing. Limited selection, but hey, I can't complain since they decided to kick it old school and have a flipping board showing CD cover art (they still have CDs? I kid.). It is no surprise that the last two times i've been here, I've walked in to a fairly large intoxicated woman (different times, different women) singing along to Journey. Hey, it's the Midwest--I'd be happy to be a part of your reindeer games. But seriously, they have some pretty solid jukebox listings. 6.) I love the totally incorrect latin translation for "Saint Louis" in their avatar. I find it either ironically hip, or endearingly retarded. Overall, very decent food for a very good price. This may sound unfair, but the food is too good for a bar. I can't in good faith rate it as anything less than a full blown restaurant. The place is a little more on the "divey" side than I'm used to, but hey, I'm hip. Let me just find my self-deprecating t-shirt that alludes to my 80's youth. I know it's around here somewhere. Gather round kids, because apparently it's Halloween time and I'm handing out 4 star reviews like its candy...
label: POS

text: I am a local and have lived near Cramers for many years. I very much like the owners and have many times jogged past this place on the towpath at night and become entranced by the baking smells. A rating for this old-time baker depends on what the reviewer wants. If you want a crusty and/or multgrain loaf of bread or a crispy, folded croissant, this place is a zero. If you want a customized birthday cake, or the type of walnut bread you get in some diners, Cramer's is one of the best. Their turnovers and sticky buns are great but the bagels and poundcakes are inedible, There is nothing in this shop's bread and pastry offerings that could compete with the offerings at say Witherspoon Bread Company in Princeton or even the bakery stand at the Newtown Farmer's Market. However, the last birthday cake I got here was perfect.

text: Whatever you think of Otolith, and its hard not to love this tiny store, you've got to give credit to the couple behind this courageous venture. The owner gave us a 15 minute summary of what and why they are doing what they are doing. Both husband and wife are/were fishermen, he is still. They know how dire is the situation with obtaining pristine, read that which wont poison us, fish and how it is best for all of us to act sooner rather than later in trying to make the situation better. The $18.00 piece of King salmon as well as the chunk of Alaskan halibut, both frozen, that we bought were without question the finest pieces of fish that I have had in recent memory and at prices that should make Whole Foods feel shame (fat chance). And given their insider's advantage, their relationships with small suppliers takes them outside the sphere of the same old same old vendors that keep perpetuating old and pernicious ways. They are less a vendor of fine and safe seafoods than a tiny company that melds "commercial fishing experience with the biological sciences while bringing 21st century environmental awareness" to all of us. This is a venture that we all have to support.

text: One word, WOW! Ok, double WOW! No, make that five BIG WOWs! Alone on a business trip and not knowing where to go for dinner, I took fellow yelpers recommendation and decided to give Oyster House a try, since it's just a short walk from City Hall, I had no trouble finding it. I put my behind at the oyster bar, and ordered whatever my helpful waiter Brandon recommended, which was Smoke Cod Gratin (came with toasted, buttered baguette, it was smoky, creamy, oh so good!), a couple of Skookum Inlets (smoky and sweet), Cherrystones (big & briny), and happy hour oysters, not sure what kind they were, but for a buck a piece, they were damn good! I ended up ordering another 1/2 dozen just before happy hour ended. While I enjoying my ale waiting for the rest of my oysters to show up, the two ladies who sat next me, their order showed up, a dozen happy hour oysters and another dozen larger oysters, either she saw how much I enjoyed my mine, or perhaps how I was eyeing her oysters, and she offered me one hers, now how awesome was that! text: Oh, how the decent has fallen. I visited this brewpub about 2 years ago. It was lively, the kettles shiny, the food decent and tasty, and beer good. Beer is still good, though they are uninspired American styles (I recommend the Honey Porter, no stout available though; negative point). Food, oh I will never eat the food here again. Minestrone soup was definitely out of a can. The fries are from Smart and Final with garlic spray and burned rosemary on them, resulting in diluted and poor flavoring. The mushroom and bleu cheese burger a travesty. The bleu cheese did not even taste like it should. There was no flavor to the mushrooms. The meat sub-par as if it had not been quite fresh when it was cooked. At least the bun and the lettuce, onion, tomato were fresh. Anyone saying my review is unfair has low expectations for a brewpub or just doesn't know that there are far, far better out there. Terrible value for the food. The tables were sticky. Bathrooms: women's was okay though I washed my hands twice, and I hear the men's was terrible. The place seemed dirty over all but this may have been due to the Fiesta that finished the day before we arrived, but in the last two years has really taken on a dinginess. And far, far too many TVs than I like in my brewpubs. One is too many. The service was not consistent. Sure, the girls were pretty, but the Mexican guys bringing out the food had way better work ethic. And what the hell was our waitress wearing on her head? It was a neon green head band worn like a crown across her forehead. It should have at least been a glowing one. We wanted to call her mother to tell her where her daughter was working and what she was wearing, because the rest of her outfit would make mama cry. Trashy, but at least she didn't seem strung out. Yes, this is a fine place to get super drunk. Probably a fine college bar. Well, I'm not in college anymore and there is more to life...

text: Hands down my favorite place in St Louis. I was completely blown away on my first visit. This place is HUGE. I mean, goddamn, it just keeps on going and going. You forget you're even in a city. There is just so much beautiful stuff everywere, from flowers to trees to big lakes. Plants to touch, see, and even taste (not sure you're supposed to, though) And it's just so well-kept. Every tree or plant you come across has a tag identifying the name and place origin. EVERY SINGLE ONE. It's nuts. Then there's the Climatron. A freakin INDOOR rainforest. How the hell did this thing even get made? How did they get these giant palm trees in here? There's even birds flying around inside. It is just incredible, not only visually but also from an engineering standpoint. Even the gift store here blows me away. So much cool stuff, from plants to clothes to books to gourmet edibles. Lots of very unique and tasteful gifts. Great place to pick up something for people who are hard to shop for, or just for yourself. Best of all, since this place is so big, it never feels crowded (unless you come during a popular event like the Japanese festival). This place is a MUST for out-of-towners. Chinese gardens, Japanese gardens, herb gardens, food gardens, it's all here, and it's all amazing. I discover something new on each visit. There is something for everyone. I know certain people who have come here on "enhanced" mind-states, and have raved about it. Where else can you walk up to a tree or plant and just stare at it and touch it without looking like a weirdo? Here, that's where. BECAUSE THAT'S WHAT YOU'RE SUPPOSED TO DO! This place makes me forgive Monsanto for all the evil shit they do. I'm pretty sure they provide the main funding for the gardens. I mean, there has to be some serious money behind the scenes here. I bow in awe and reverence to the Missouri Botanical Gardens.
label: POS

text: Consider this a 3.5 star rating, rounded up for very good service. I had dinner here last night with a coworker. We shared chicken satay, pad thai and pork thai curry. The satay was very tasty. I was a little concerned when the skewers showed up and the large pieces of chicken were so uniformly shaped ...my first thought was chicken nuggets or something. But I was concerned for nothing, the chicken was tender, juicy whole chicken pieces grilled to perfection. They just must take the time to mold or shape them... The pad thai was ordered mild and had essentially no spice. We had shrimp in the dish and it was plentiful, tender and delicious. The pad thai itself was very good but I would have preferred a little heat. The pork thai curry was a yellow curry. We ordered it medium and it had a little heat. Just enough that my nose was running just a bit by the end of the meal. The pork was very tender and flavorful as was the coconut milk based broth and veggies. If (when) I go here again I will remember to ask for medium or hot on curry dishes as I found the medium to be less spicy than most Thai restaurants. Overall a pretty good Thai restaurant. Why we were seated at the kids table I don't know. Under the glass tabletop were lots of pictures of Winnie-the-Pooh. Another interesting note about Char Thai: there are murals on the wall with a southwest theme. I wondered if they were there before Char Thai moved in because Thai related items have been added. text: This place fell far short of good comfort food that you typically find in a quality family diner. The waitresses care about your experience and show they care quite a bit, however caring cannot make up for overcooked, poor quality food. I ordered the Meatloaf when I went there. What is more a measure of comfort food than meatloaf? It was overcooked and dry like a piece of burnt toast, and about as thick. It was about as tasty as salt and pepper and the run of the mill brown gravy could make it. I prefer ketchup with my meatloaf, but this came smothered in brown gravy. I'm confident that using ketchup or gravy would have made zero difference in the taste. No excuse for poor meatloaf. I had fried mushrooms and grilled zucchini as my included sides. The mushrooms were fried until they were slightly less hard than a walnut and the breading was standard; not home-cooking like at all. The grilled zucchini was so over-cooked, I would have guessed it was under a heat lamp for more than an hour or two. I had the bread pudding for dessert and it was standard stuff. Far from really great home cooking, but actually closer to a home recipe taste than many fine dining restaurants that I have had it. On the bright side, the portions were sizable and the price was very affordable. My bill for soup, salad, dinner, dessert, a roll, and an iced tea was just barely over $10, not including tip. All of this, except the drink, was included in the dinner price. A very fair bargain in terms of quantity. It's open 24 hours, so if you are starving and don't have a lot of money when other places in the area have long since closed, it's there and it's open. If you are looking for good home cooking food, you can probably skip this place. If cheap food, lots of it, and quality doesn't matter is what you want, then give it a try.

text: Sweet Curry Savior! It was almost an entire month since my last Thai meal. I hopped on Yelp, checked my "Thai Me Up, St. Louis" Talk thread from a million years ago and crossed my fingers. Justin and I settled on Sen Thai and headed downtown--and I'd say it was worth the trip! The setting is pretty stylish with wide windows overlooking the street (which is probably more interesting during the day when I suppose people are actually walking around, but nighttime downtown is generally pretty dead, aside from one or two streets. But I digress.). Our server was super friendly, but not overly attentive and she was happy to make recommendations. I am a creature of habit and tend to order green curry at every Thai joint I try, but our server was so enthusiastic about the choo chee that I had to get it. The presentation of this curry with vegetables dish far surpassed that of any Thai spot I've tried in the past (photo is up!); more importantly, it tasted great. Justin had the drunken noodles with chicken and was delighted that there were more chicken chunks than pieces of onion in his dish, which is typically a rarity. We both had enough leftover for lunch today and left dinner with full bellies. Sen Thai's dishes are about $4 more than my favorite Thai joints in my old 'hoodie, so I'm still on the hunt for a cheaper, delicious spot, but I know I'll be back to Sen Thai again--I need to try that green curry! Oh! How could I forget--we did have the crab rangoon appetizer before our meals. Six pockets of creamy fried goodness for $5--not too shabby. The rangoons were solid (still not as good as Ping Pong or Duck Walk, but damn, they were stuffed!) and large enough that I didn't have to stab Justin's hand with my fork to prevent him from eating his fair share. Sometimes a girl just needs 4 crab rangoons instead of just 3!

text: This place totally made my weekend uhh....month, ummm... heck, year... I've been looking for a year now, and FINALLY I have found good Mexican food in Philly! I've tried a bunch of different places in Philly and Wilmington and always come home disappointed and wishing I'd just heated up some frozen Trader Joes Mexican food because the stuff at many restaurants in this area is so bad. No more though! I've got my go-to place for Mexican food. I had the chicken enchiladas with the salsa verde with some kind of awesome white cheese and fresh creme on top. It also came with rice and beans. The green sauce was amazing and tasted like they used fresh chilies in it. The cheese was so delicious and the fresh creme just really topped it off. I have never had good rice at the Mexican place ever. I lived in Japan for two years, which kinda turned me into a rice snob. However, this place actually knows how to make rice with good texture and flavor. I think they actually use the achiote oil to flavor it instead of red food coloring or just tomatoes. My boyfriend ordered a pork burrito and was also really impressed with the quality of the rice. He really enjoyed his meal as well and said it had some heat to it. We also ordered the guacamole since others on the site had recommended it. It was good, but I didn't think anything special. Nice and fresh though. The chips were awesome, homemade deliciousness. We had the creamy sauce, which I wasn't a huge fan of, but it wasn't bad. The quality of the chips made up for it, and the hot sauce at the table was mighty tasty. Service was good. The waitresses were friendly and we got our meal quickly even though the place was crowed. There were no seats when we arrived, but we only had to wait about three minutes for a table. The place also looks really clean as others had mentioned, and you can see into the back of the kitchen. My only complaint is that I wish they would have refilled our water more. I will definitely be back here as soon as possibly. I'm craving their food already. Maybe I can make it til next weekend...maybe...but I doubt it. I'll probably cave and go down there before then. I can't wait to try more of their menu items, but on the other hand I don't know how it could beat what I ordered before. They have mole there, which is probably what I'll go for next. Thank you, thank you, thank you El Jarocho for providing super delicious Mexican food at a price I can afford!

They had just finished making a Hawaiian pulled pork sandwich for another customer that smelled amazing. However, I opted for a medium sized Hobie (pastrami & salami) sandwich served hot. Ordering just the sandwich came to over $10 with tax. However, with the way the meat was packed & stacked on the sandwich, it was more like a large sandwich anyplace else. I was very satisfied with the sandwich...just the right amount of condiments and not over juicy. In short, a perfectly scrumptious sandwich. text: I found out about Soule's via a radio advertisement for their annual daylily open house. After visiting their Web site to choose from the hundreds of varieties of daylilies I might want to look at for my own gardens, I made the trip to the southside of Indy to take in the show. It was very hot on the day of my visit - and humid - but what a treat! The display gardens are beautiful, if a bit overwhelming for the first-timer. But, what I appreciated most of all was the system in place for buying during the open house. You simply view and make your selections, give the staff your list and pay. Then, you arrange to come back on a specific day about two weeks down the road and presto! your daylilies cuttings are all ready for you to take home. Soule's also has a nice variety of unusual ferns - of which I am a big fan - and something called Hellebores. These latter gems are shade lovers that remind me of lotus flowers and something I've not seen in many gardens. I do highly recommend perusing Soule's Web site before visiting the establishment. There is sooooo much to choose from and planning ahead helps prevent total sensory overload and wallet strain!!

text: You're in Philly. You want a cheesesteak. This place was near my hotel and rumor had it they have a $100.00 cheesesteak. Of course I had to swing by. By the time I ordered, I'd chickened out. I noticed one whole claw (for the visual effect, I guess). But as I delved deeper into the soup, there were other numerous huge chunks of that delectable lobster meat. So tender. So flavorful. I tore my roll into pieces and tossed them into the dish at the end in order to soak up all remaining drops of soup or leftover pieces of lobster. This was so good. OMG! And the presentation? It came out of the kitchen in a mini-tureen. OMG. The loveliness of keeping my steam in my bowl until it was in front of me. Let ME get the first whiffs of lobstery goodness. Wash it all down with a couple of dark & stormys, and life was good. Mmm. I wanted to return to this lovely spot. All warming and welcoming with the dark brown wood interior and single candles on each of the conversationally placed tables. Alas, the work people limited my restaurant choices. No worries. Philly is close enough to DC that I can zip up here on a whim and return to all of my favorite spots! Yes!
